Figure 8:

Illustration of Eq. (
143
). The incoming quark line terminated with a “
\;\scriptstyle{[}\;
” stands for
{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\,u(p,s)
and the outgoing terminated quark line stands for
\bar{u}(p,s)\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}
. These factors do not vanish as long as
p^{2}\neq 0
.

We can also determine how
R_{\mathrm{q}}
depends on the gauge parameters
r_{i}
. We start with

\frac{\partial G(p)}{\partial r_{i}}\sim\frac{{\mathrm{i}}{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}}{p^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0}\ \frac{\partial R_{\mathrm{q}}(p)}{\partial r_{i}}

(141)

Then the steps in Eq. (
139
) give us

{\mathrm{i}}p^{2}\,\frac{\partial R_{\mathrm{q}}(p)}{\partial r_{i}}\sim\bar{u}(p,s)\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\,\frac{\partial G(p)}{\partial r_{i}}\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\,u(p,s)\;.

(142)

To obtain
\partial G(p)/\partial r_{i}
we use the identity (
102
). There are contributions from both ends of the quark propagator. The contribution for the right end has a vertex that combines a quark with momentum
p-k
and Lorentz index
\beta
with a ghost with momentum
k
, with no attached gluon propagator. The contribution for the left end has a vertex that combines an incoming quark with momentum
p+k
and Lorentz index
\alpha
with a ghost that supplies momentum
k
, with no attached quark propagator. We can write these contributions as

\begin{split}\frac{\partial R_{\mathrm{q}}(p)}{\partial r_{i}}\sim{}&\frac{-{\mathrm{i}}}{p^{2}}\,\bar{u}(p,s){\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\,\big[G(p)\,\Gamma(p)+\overline{\Gamma}(-p)\,G(p)\big]\\
&\times{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\,u(p,s)\;.\end{split}

(143)

This equation is illustrated in Fig.
8
.

The Dirac structure of
\Gamma
can be specified. We note that
\Gamma
contains an even number of
\gamma
-matrices and is a function of
p
and
n
. It thus has the form

\begin{split}\Gamma={}&\Gamma_{\!\mathrm{q}}\,1+\frac{\Gamma^{\prime}_{\!\mathrm{q}}}{p^{2}}\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{0}{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\;.\end{split}

(144)

Here
\Gamma_{\!\mathrm{q}}(p)
and
\Gamma_{\!\mathrm{q}}^{\prime}(p)
are a scalar functions of
p
and
n
.

Now, using
{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{0}\,u(p,s)=0
,

\begin{split}\Gamma\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\,u(p,s)={}&\Gamma_{\!\mathrm{q}}\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\,u(p,s)+\Gamma^{\prime}_{\!\mathrm{q}}\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{0}\,u(p,s)\\
={}&\Gamma_{\!\mathrm{q}}\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\,u(p,s)\;.\end{split}

(145)

Similarly,

\begin{split}\bar{u}(p,s)\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\,\overline{\Gamma}={}&\Gamma_{\!\mathrm{q}}\,\bar{u}(p,s)\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\;.\end{split}

(146)

Now Eq. (
143
) becomes

\begin{split}\frac{\partial R_{\mathrm{q}}(p)}{\partial r_{i}}\sim{}&\frac{-{\mathrm{i}}}{p^{2}}\,\bar{u}(p,s){\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\,G(p){\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\,u(p,s)\ 2\Gamma_{\!\mathrm{q}}\;.\end{split}

(147)

Using Eq. (
140
) then gives

\begin{split}\frac{\partial R_{\mathrm{q}}(p)}{\partial r_{i}}={}&2R_{\mathrm{q}}(p)\,\Gamma_{\!\mathrm{q}}(p)\;.\end{split}

(148)

The same analysis applies to antiquarks, with the same function
\Gamma_{\mathrm{q}}
.

V.6
Dependence of the S matrix on the
r_{i}

We have seen in subsection
V.3
how a Green function for gluons, quarks, and antiquarks depends on the gauge parameters
r_{i}
defined in Eq. (
86
). We can use this result to find how the S matrix depends on the
r_{i}
. Let us call the Green function in momentum space
G(p_{1},\mu_{1},a_{1};p_{2},\alpha_{2},i_{2};p_{3},\beta_{3},j_{3};\dots)
. Here the gluon with momentum
p_{1}
has vector index
\mu_{1}
and color
\bm{8}
index
a_{1}
; the quark with momentum
p_{2}
has Dirac index
\alpha_{2}
and color
\bm{3}
index
i_{2}
; the antiquark with momentum
p_{3}
has Dirac index
\beta_{3}
and color
\bar{\bm{3}}
index
j_{3}
. There can be more partons, indicted by the ellipsis. All momenta are defined to be outgoing.

From the Green function, we can construct the S matrix
S(p_{1},s_{1},a_{1};p_{2},s_{2},i_{2};p_{3},s_{3},j_{3};\dots)
. We start with off-shell partons with momenta
p_{j}
, but we will then take a limit
p_{j}^{2}\to 0
. The variables
s_{i}
label the transverse polarizations of the gluons or the spins of the quarks or antiquarks. The S matrix is related to the Green function by

\displaystyle S(p_{1},

\displaystyle s_{1},a_{1};p_{2},s_{2},i_{2};p_{3},s_{3},j_{3};\dots)

\displaystyle={}

\displaystyle G(p_{1},\mu_{1},a_{1};p_{2},\alpha_{2},i_{2};p_{3},\beta_{3},j_{3};\dots)

\displaystyle\times\frac{({\mathrm{i}}p_{1}^{2})\,\varepsilon_{\mu_{1}}(p_{1},s_{1})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{g}}(p_{1})}}\,\frac{\overline{u}_{\alpha_{2}}(p_{2},s_{2})\,(-{\mathrm{i}}{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{2})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{2})}}

(149)

\displaystyle\times\frac{(-{\mathrm{i}}{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{3})\,v_{\beta_{3}}(p_{3},s_{3})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{3})}}\times\cdots\;.

This definition applies using the renormalized Green function
G
and the factors
R
in
4-2\epsilon
dimensions, with infrared divergences regulated by keeping
\epsilon<0
, as in Eq. (
112
). For quarks and antiquarks, we have multiplied by an inverse tree level propagator,
-{\mathrm{i}}{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}
. For each parton, we have multiplied by the appropriate polarization vector or spinor, with an implied sum over the polarization or spinor index. (This is for final state quarks and antiquarks. The choice is modified for initial state antiquarks or quarks.) The polarization vectors and spinors are functions of the parts of the momenta
p_{1}
,
p_{2}
, and
p_{3}
that are orthogonal to
n
, as in Sec.
V.5
. Thus
\overline{u}_{\alpha_{2}}(p_{2},s_{2}){\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{2}
and
{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{3}v_{\alpha_{2}}(p_{3},s_{3})
do not vanish as long as
p_{2}^{2}
and
p_{3}^{2}
are not zero.

In
G
, the propagator for T gluons,
G_{\mathrm{T}}
(Eq. (
124
)) multiplies
\varepsilon_{\mu_{1}}(p_{1},s_{1})
. The propagator for L gluons,
G_{\mathrm{L}}
, does not appear because it lacks poles
1/p_{1}^{2}
. We will differentiate
S
with respect to the gauge parameters
r_{i}
. Four of these parameters are the components of
n
. The polarization vector
\varepsilon_{\mu_{1}}(p_{1},s_{1})
depends on
n
. However, the derivative of
\varepsilon_{\mu_{1}}(p_{1},s_{1})
with respect to
n_{\alpha}
gives zero when contracted with
G_{\mathrm{T}}
, as we saw in Eq. (
127
). Thus we can treat
\varepsilon_{\mu_{1}}(p_{1},s_{1})
as if it were independent of all of the
r_{i}
.

In Eq. (
V.6
), we have started with the full Green function and divided by a factor
\sqrt{R}
for each external leg. An alternative formulation, which we use later in this paper, is to divide by
R
for each external leg, giving the Green function amputated on the external legs, then to multiply by
\sqrt{R}
.

We would now like to see how the S matrix depends on the gauge parameters. We differentiate
S
with respect to the gauge parameter
r_{i}
. Here we have to differentiate both
G
and each factor of
1/\sqrt{R}
. We get

\begin{split}\frac{\partial S}{\partial r_{i}}={}&\frac{\partial G}{\partial r_{i}}\,\frac{({\mathrm{i}}p_{1}^{2})\,\varepsilon_{\mu_{1}}(p_{1},s_{1})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{g}}(p_{1})}}\,\frac{\overline{u}_{\alpha_{2}}(p_{2},s_{2})\,(-{\mathrm{i}}{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{2})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{2})}}\,\frac{(-{\mathrm{i}}{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{3})\,v_{\beta_{3}}(p_{3},s_{3})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{q}(p_{3})}}}\times\cdots\\
&-G\left[\frac{({\mathrm{i}}p_{1}^{2})\,\varepsilon_{\mu_{1}}(p_{1},s_{1})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{g}}(p_{1})}}\,\frac{\overline{u}_{\alpha_{2}}(p_{2},s_{2})\,(-{\mathrm{i}}{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{2})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{2})}}\,\frac{(-{\mathrm{i}}{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{3})\,v_{\beta_{3}}(p_{3},s_{3})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{3})}}\times\cdots\right]\\
&\times\left[\frac{1}{2R_{\mathrm{g}}(p_{1})}\frac{\partial R_{\mathrm{g}}(p_{1})}{\partial r_{i}}+\frac{1}{2R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{2})}\frac{\partial R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{2})}{\partial r_{i}}+\frac{1}{2R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{3})}\frac{\partial R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{3})}{\partial r_{i}}+\cdots\right]\;.\end{split}

(150)

Let us examine the term in Eq. (
150
) proportional to
\partial G/\partial r_{i}
. There is a term in
\partial G/\partial r_{i}
, represented as the first term in Fig.
5
, that is proportional to
p_{1}^{\mu_{1}}
. This term does not contribute to Eq. (
150
) because
p_{1}\cdot\varepsilon(p_{1},s_{1})=0
.

In the next term in
\partial G/\partial r_{i}
, a gluon with momentum
p_{1}-k
joins a ghost with momentum
k
at a vertex
V_{\mathrm{g}}
, Eq. (
108
). There is no subsequent propagator with a factor
1/p_{1}^{2}
. Since we multiply by
p_{1}^{2}
in Eq. (
150
), this contribution vanishes when we take
p_{1}^{2}\to 0
for many of the graphs that contribute to
\partial G/\partial r_{i}
. However, there are some graphs in which a gluon line carrying momentum
p_{1}
enters a one-particle irreducible subgraph
\Gamma
that involves the special gluon-ghost mixing vertex together with other interactions and finally creates a gluon and a ghost that combine in the vertex
V_{\mathrm{g}}
. This single gluon propagator has a factor
1/p_{1}^{2}
that cancels the factor
p_{1}^{2}
to give us a finite contribution when
p_{1}^{2}\to 0
. After analyzing the structure of the one-particle-irreducible graphs as in Sec.
V.5
, we obtain a contribution of the form

G\,\frac{{\mathrm{i}}p_{1}^{2}\varepsilon_{\mu_{1}}(p_{1},s_{1})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{g}}(p_{1})}}\ \Gamma_{\!\mathrm{g}}\;.

(151)

In the next term in
\partial G/\partial r_{i}
, a quark with momentum
p_{2}-k
joins a ghost with momentum
k
at a vertex
V_{\mathrm{q}}
, Eq. (
105
). There is no subsequent propagator with a factor
{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{2}/p_{2}^{2}
. Thus this contribution vanishes when we take
p_{2}^{2}\to 0
for many graphs. However, there are some graphs in which a quark line carrying momentum
p_{2}
enters a one-particle-irreducible subgraph that involves the special gluon-ghost mixing vertex together with other interactions and finally creates a quark and a ghost that combine in the vertex
V_{\mathrm{q}}
. This single gluon propagator has a factor
{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{2}/p_{2}^{2}
that gives us a finite contribution when
p_{2}^{2}\to 0
. After analyzing the structure of the one-particle-irreducible graphs as in Sec.
V.5
, we obtain a contribution of the form

G\,\frac{\overline{u}_{\alpha_{2}}(p_{2},s_{2})\,(-{\mathrm{i}}{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{2})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{2})}}\ \Gamma_{\!\mathrm{q}}\;.

(152)

In the next term in
\partial G/\partial r_{i}
, an antiquark with momentum
p_{3}-k
joins a ghost with momentum
k
at a vertex
V_{\bar{\mathrm{q}}}
, Eq. (
106
). The surviving contributions come from one-particle-irreducible subgraphs coupled to a full Green function. As in the quark case, these give a contribution

G\,\frac{(-{\mathrm{i}}{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{3})\,v_{\beta_{3}}(p_{3},s_{3})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{3})}}\ \Gamma_{\!\mathrm{q}}\;.

(153)

Summing these contributions, we have

\begin{split}\frac{\partial S}{\partial r_{i}}={}&G\left[\frac{({\mathrm{i}}p_{1}^{2})\,\varepsilon_{\mu_{1}}(p_{1},s_{1})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{g}}(p_{1})}}\,\frac{\overline{u}_{\alpha_{2}}(p_{2},s_{2})\,(-{\mathrm{i}}{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{2})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{2})}}\,\frac{(-{\mathrm{i}}{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}_{3})\,v_{\beta_{3}}(p_{3},s_{3})}{\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{3})}}\times\cdots\right]\\
&\times\left[\Gamma_{\!\mathrm{g}}-\frac{1}{2R_{\mathrm{g}}(p_{1})}\frac{\partial R_{\mathrm{g}}(p_{1})}{\partial r_{i}}+\Gamma_{\!\mathrm{q}}-\frac{1}{2R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{2})}\frac{\partial R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{2})}{\partial r_{i}}+\Gamma_{\!\mathrm{q}}-\frac{1}{2R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{3})}\frac{\partial R_{\mathrm{q}}(p_{3})}{\partial r_{i}}+\cdots\right]\;.\end{split}

(154)

In Sec.
V.5
, we found the derivatives of
R_{\mathrm{g}}
and
R_{\mathrm{q}}
with respect to
r_{i}
:

\begin{split}\Gamma_{\!\mathrm{g}}={}&\frac{1}{2R_{\mathrm{g}}}\frac{\partial R_{\mathrm{g}}}{\partial r_{i}}\;,\\
\Gamma_{\!\mathrm{q}}={}&\frac{1}{2R_{\mathrm{q}}}\frac{\partial R_{\mathrm{q}}}{\partial r_{i}}\;.\end{split}

(155)

Inserting this into Eq. (
154
), we find that the S matrix is invariant under changes of the gauge parameters,

\frac{\partial S}{\partial r_{i}}=0\;.

(156)

VI
Renormalization

Ref.
BaulieuZwanziger
provided an argument, based on BRST invariance, that QCD in interpolating gauge can be renormalized. In this section, we calculate the one-loop contributions to the renormalization factors
Z
.

To renormalize the theory in interpolating gauge, we need to renormalize the coupling
g
, the gauge parameters
v
and
\xi
, and the field strengths. In each case, we relate a “bare” quantity, indicated with a subscript B, to a corresponding renormalized quantity by means of a factor
Z
or
\sqrt{Z}
. In the case of the gluon field,
\sqrt{Z}
is a matrix. Each of the
Z
factors depend on
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
and the gauge parameters
v^{2}
and
\xi
. We expand the
Z
factors in powers of
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
, beginning with 1 or the unit matrix at order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{0}
. In this section, we examine the
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{1}
contributions.

The field strength renormalizations take the form

\begin{split}A^{\mu}_{a}(x)_{\mathrm{B}}={}&[Z_{A}^{1/2}]^{\mu}_{\nu}\,A^{\nu}_{a}(x)\;,\\
\psi_{\alpha}(x)_{\mathrm{B}}={}&Z_{\psi}^{1/2}\,\psi_{\alpha}(x)\;,\\
\bar{\psi}_{\alpha}(x)_{\mathrm{B}}={}&Z_{\psi}^{1/2}\,\bar{\psi}_{\alpha}(x)\;,\\
\eta_{a}(x)_{\mathrm{B}}={}&Z_{\eta}^{1/2}\,\eta_{a}(x)\;,\\
\bar{\eta}_{a}(x)_{\mathrm{B}}={}&Z_{\eta}^{1/2}\,\bar{\eta}_{a}(x)\;.\end{split}

(157)

The field strength renormalization factor for the gluon field needs to be a Lorentz tensor instead of just a scalar because the definition of the gauge uses a fixed vector
n
. The coupling and gauge parameters are renormalized as

\begin{split}g_{\mathrm{B}}={}&Z_{g}\,g\;,\\
v^{2}_{\mathrm{B}}={}&Z_{v}\,v^{2}\;,\\
\xi_{\mathrm{B}}={}&Z_{\xi}\,\xi\;.\end{split}

(158)

VI.1
The renormalization factors

We begin with a statement of the results for the renormalization factors
Z
. In the following subsection, we exhibit the calculation that leads to these results.

At order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
, the renormalization factor for the coupling is the same as in a covariant gauge,

Z_{g}=1-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{g}}+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;,

(159)

where

\gamma_{\mathrm{g}}=\frac{11}{6}\,C_{A}-\frac{2}{3}\,T_{R}n_{f}

(160)

and
S_{\epsilon}
is the standard coefficient of
1/\epsilon
for
\overline{\mathrm{MS}}
renormalization,

S_{\epsilon}=\frac{(4\pi)^{\epsilon}}{\Gamma(1-\epsilon)}\;.

(161)

The quark field renormalization is

\begin{split}Z_{\psi}={}&1-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\left[\frac{(v-1)^{2}}{v(v+1)}+\frac{\xi}{v}\right]C_{\mathrm{F}}+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.\end{split}

(162)

The ghost field renormalization is

Z_{\eta}=1+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\left[\frac{16v^{2}+v+1}{12v(v+1)}-\frac{\xi}{4v}\right]C_{\mathrm{A}}+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.

(163)

The components of
A_{a}^{\mu}(x)
along
n
and orthogonal to
n
renormalize differently. We find

\begin{split}Z_{A}^{\mu\nu}={}&g^{\mu\nu}+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\big[c_{A}(v,\xi)\,g^{\mu\nu}+\tilde{c}_{A}(v,\xi)\,h^{\mu\nu}\big]\\
&+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;,\end{split}

(164)

where the coefficients are

\begin{split}c_{A}(v,\xi)={}&\left[\frac{22v^{3}+35v^{2}+20v-1}{6v(v+1)^{2}}-\frac{\xi}{2v}\right]C_{\mathrm{A}}\\
&\quad-\frac{4}{3}\,T_{R}n_{\mathrm{f}}\;,\\
\tilde{c}_{A}(v,\xi)={}&-\frac{4v(2v+1)}{3(v+1)^{2}}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}\;.\end{split}

(165)

Using the projections
P_{\pm}
along
n
and orthogonal to
n
defined in Eq. (
20
),
Z_{A}^{\mu\nu}
is

\begin{split}Z_{A}^{\mu\nu}={}&g^{\mu\nu}\\
&+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\bigg[\!\left(c_{A}(v,\xi)+\frac{1}{v^{2}}\,\tilde{c}_{A}(v,\xi)\right)\!P_{+}^{\mu\nu}\\
&\quad+\big(c_{A}(v,\xi)+\tilde{c}_{A}(v,\xi)\big)P_{-}^{\mu\nu}\bigg]+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.\end{split}

(166)

The renormalization factors for the gauge parameters are determined from the renormalization of the gauge field:

\begin{split}Z_{v}={}&1-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\frac{v^{2}-1}{2v^{2}}\,\tilde{c}_{A}(v,\xi)+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;,\\
Z_{\xi}={}&1+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\left[c_{A}(v,\xi)+\frac{v^{2}+1}{2v^{2}}\,\tilde{c}_{A}(v,\xi)\right]\\
&+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.\end{split}

(167)

p-q
q
p
p
q
p
p
q
p-q
p
p
p-q
q
p
p

Figure 9:

Gluon self-energy. There are four graphs: a gluon loop, a gluon tadpole, a ghost loop, and a quark loop.

VI.2
Determination of the renormalization factors

The renormalization factors
Z
at order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
can be determined by one-loop calculations. We illustrate this with the gluon propagator. Its renormalization is more complicated than in Feynman gauge because we are using a gauge condition that breaks manifest Lorentz invariance.

The inverse gluon propagator is
-{\mathrm{i}}\Gamma^{\mu\nu}(p)
with

\Gamma^{\mu\nu}(p)=\Gamma_{\mathrm{tree}}^{\mu\nu}(v,\xi;p)-\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)\;.

(168)

Here
\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)
is the gluon self-energy tensor, which we calculate at order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
using the graphs in Fig.
9
. The tree level inverse gluon propagator,

\Gamma_{\mathrm{tree}}^{\mu\nu}(v,\xi;p)=-g^{\mu\nu}p^{2}+p^{\mu}p^{\nu}-\frac{v^{2}}{\xi}\,\tilde{p}^{\mu}\tilde{p}^{\nu}\;,

(169)

depends on the gauge parameters
v
and
\xi
through the factor
v^{2}/\xi
and through the presence of
v
in the definition (
22
) of
\tilde{p}^{\mu}=h^{\mu}_{\nu}p^{\nu}
.

The parameters
v^{2}
and
\xi
are renormalized and, in addition,
\Gamma^{\mu\nu}
is renormalized according to

\Gamma^{\mu\nu}=[Z_{A}^{1/2}]^{\mu}_{\alpha}\Gamma_{\mathrm{B}}^{\alpha\beta}[Z_{A}^{1/2}]^{\nu}_{\beta}\;,

(170)

where

\Gamma^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{B}}(p)=\Gamma_{\mathrm{tree}}^{\mu\nu}(v_{\mathrm{B}},\xi_{\mathrm{B}};p)-\Pi_{\mathrm{B}}^{\mu\nu}(p)\;.

(171)

We calculate
\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{B}}
in the bare theory from the diagrams in Fig.
9
. However, in this calculation we substitute the renormalized versions of
g
,
v^{2}
, and
\xi
for their bare versions since
\Pi^{\mu\nu}
is already of order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
. Then
\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{B}}
thus calculated will contain ultraviolet (UV) poles
1/\epsilon
. The renormalization program will remove these poles.

We write
[Z_{A}^{1/2}]^{\mu\nu}
to first order in the form

[Z_{A}^{1/2}]^{\mu\nu}=g^{\mu\nu}+\frac{1}{2}\delta Z_{I}\,g^{\mu\nu}+\frac{1}{2}\delta Z_{h}\,h^{\mu\nu}+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.

(172)

(The subscript
I
on
\delta Z_{I}
refers to the fact that the metric tensor acts as the identity operator on vectors:
g^{\mu}_{\alpha}p^{\alpha}=p^{\mu}
.) After using Eq. (
23
), we find for the counterterms from
Z_{A}
:

\displaystyle\Gamma^{\mu\nu}={}

\displaystyle\Gamma^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{B}}-(\delta Z_{I}g^{\mu\nu}+\delta Z_{h}h^{\mu\nu})p^{2}

\displaystyle+\delta Z_{I}p^{\mu}p^{\nu}+\frac{\xi+1}{2\xi}\delta Z_{h}(p^{\mu}\tilde{p}^{\nu}+\tilde{p}^{\mu}p^{\nu})

(173)

\displaystyle-\left[\frac{v^{2}}{\xi}\delta Z_{I}+\frac{v^{2}+1}{\xi}\delta Z_{h}\right]\tilde{p}^{\mu}\tilde{p}^{\nu}+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.

There are also counterterms from the renormalization of
v^{2}
and
\xi
:

\begin{split}v^{2}_{\mathrm{B}}={}&v^{2}+\delta Z_{v}v^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}})\;,\\
\xi_{\mathrm{B}}={}&\xi+\delta Z_{\xi}\xi+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}})\;.\end{split}

(174)

When we account for the direct appearance of
v^{2}
and
\xi
in Eq. (
169
) and the appearance of
v^{2}
in
\tilde{p}^{\lambda}=h^{\lambda}_{\alpha}p^{\alpha}
, these relations give us

\begin{split}\Gamma^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{B}}={}&\Gamma^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{tree}}(v_{\mathrm{B}},\xi_{\mathrm{B}};p)-\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{B}}\\
={}&\Gamma^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{tree}}(v,\xi;p)-\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{B}}+\frac{v^{2}}{\xi}\,\frac{1}{v^{2}-1}\,\delta Z_{v}(p^{\mu}\tilde{p}^{\nu}+\tilde{p}^{\mu}p^{\nu})+\frac{v^{2}}{\xi}\,\left[\delta Z_{\xi}-\frac{v^{2}+1}{v^{2}-1}\,\delta Z_{v}\right]\tilde{p}^{\mu}\tilde{p}^{\nu}+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.\end{split}

(175)

We substitute
\Gamma^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{B}}
from Eq. (
175
) into Eq. (
VI.2
) for
\Gamma^{\mu\nu}
. Then
\Gamma^{\mu\nu}=\Gamma^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{tree}}-\Pi^{\mu\nu}
is

\begin{split}\Gamma^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{tree}}(v,\xi;p)-\Pi^{\mu\nu}={}&\Gamma^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{tree}}(v,\xi;p)-\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{B}}-\delta Z_{I}(g^{\mu\nu}p^{2}-p^{\mu}p^{\nu})-\delta Z_{h}h^{\mu\nu}p^{2}\\
&+\left[\frac{\xi+1}{2\xi}\delta Z_{h}+\frac{v^{2}}{\xi}\,\frac{1}{v^{2}-1}\,\delta Z_{v}\right](p^{\mu}\tilde{p}^{\nu}+\tilde{p}^{\mu}p^{\nu})\\
&-\left[\frac{v^{2}}{\xi}\delta Z_{I}+\frac{v^{2}+1}{\xi}\delta Z_{h}-\frac{v^{2}}{\xi}\,\delta Z_{\xi}+\frac{v^{2}}{\xi}\,\frac{v^{2}+1}{v^{2}-1}\,\delta Z_{v}\right]\tilde{p}^{\mu}\tilde{p}^{\nu}+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.\end{split}

(176)

We note that the terms
\Gamma^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{tree}}(v,\xi;p)
cancel in Eq. (
176
). The renormalized one loop gluon self-energy,
\Pi^{\mu\nu}
, should not have ultraviolet poles. We calculate the ultraviolet poles in
\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{B}}(p)
at order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
from the diagrams in Fig.
9
, giving

\begin{split}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{B}}(p)={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\Bigg\{-c_{A}(v,\xi)\big[p^{2}\,g^{\mu\nu}-p^{\mu}p^{\nu}\big]\\
&-\tilde{c}_{A}(v,\xi)\,h^{\mu\nu}p^{2}+\frac{\tilde{c}_{A}(v,\xi)}{2}\,\big[p^{\mu}\tilde{p}^{\nu}+\tilde{p}^{\mu}p^{\nu}\big]\Bigg\}\\
&\times\left(1+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)\right)+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;,\end{split}

(177)

where
c_{A}(v,\xi)
and
\tilde{c}_{A}(v,\xi)
are given in Eq. (
165
). Evidently, the pole proportional to
p^{2}g^{\mu\nu}-p^{\mu}p^{\nu}
is removed if we choose

\delta Z_{I}=\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,c_{A}(v,\xi)\;.

(178)

The pole proportional to
h^{\mu\nu}p^{2}
is removed if we choose

\delta Z_{h}=\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\tilde{c}_{A}(v,\xi)\;.

(179)

Then the pole proportional to
p^{\mu}\tilde{p}^{\nu}+\tilde{p}^{\mu}p^{\nu}
is removed if we choose

\delta Z_{v}=-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\frac{v^{2}-1}{2v^{2}}\,\tilde{c}_{A}(v,\xi)\;.

(180)

There is no pole proportional to
\tilde{p}^{\mu}\tilde{p}^{\nu}
. This can be arranged if we choose

\delta Z_{\xi}=\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\left[c_{A}(v,\xi)+\frac{v^{2}+1}{2v^{2}}\,\tilde{c}_{A}(v,\xi)\right]\;.

(181)

This calculation gives the order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
results given in Eq. (
164
) and (
167
).

VII
The gluon self-energy

In Appendix
B
, we use the diagrams in Fig.
9
to calculate the one loop gluon self-energy
\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)
with
\overline{\mathrm{MS}}
renormalization with
\xi=1
and
p^{2}<0
. We express the unrenormalized
\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)
as an integral over Feynman parameters and as an integral in
d=4-2\epsilon
dimensions over the loop momentum. The integral over the loop momentum can then be performed analytically. This gives terms with UV poles
1/\epsilon
. The pole terms are reported in Eq. (
177
). (In Eq. (
177
), we have added a calculation of the UV poles for
\xi\neq 1
.) The UV poles are removed by
\overline{\mathrm{MS}}
renormalization, as described in Sec.
VI
. This gives the renormalized
\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)
.

The gluon self-energy has the decomposition

\begin{split}\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\big\{A_{1}p^{2}g^{\mu\nu}+A_{2}p^{2}h^{\mu\nu}+A_{3}p^{\mu}p^{\nu}\\
&\quad+A_{4}\tilde{p}^{\mu}\tilde{p}^{\nu}+A_{5}(p^{\mu}\tilde{p}^{\nu}+\tilde{p}^{\mu}p^{\nu})\big\}\;.\end{split}

(182)

The coefficients
A_{i}
are given as integrals over Feynman parameters. Using the Feynman rules to construct the graphs for the first order gluon self-energy function, we see that it obeys the identity

p_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)\,p_{\nu}=0\;.

(183)

This implies that there is a linear relation among the five coefficients
A_{i}
. When the
A_{i}
are computed numerically, this relation provides a check on the calculation.

Of special importance are S-matrix elements involving an initial or final state T gluon. In this case, the final gluon propagator is amputated and we take
p^{2}\to 0
and multiply by a polarization vector
\varepsilon^{\mu}(p,s)
. According to Eq. (
V.6
), in the case that there is a self-energy insertion on the gluon line, we multiply the one particle irreducible subgraph by the LSZ factor
\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{g}}}
. Using Eq. (
112
) for
R_{\mathrm{g}}
, we derive

\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{g}}(p)}-1=\left[\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}\right]_{p^{2}\to 0}+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.

(184)

This quantity has IR divergences. We define
R_{\mathrm{g}}
from the renormalized
\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)
by taking the
p^{2}\to 0
limit with dimensional regulation to control the IR divergences. Then we take
\epsilon\to 0
, obtaining
1/\epsilon^{2}
and
1/\epsilon
IR poles plus finite terms. The calculation, with
\xi=1
, is described in Appendix
C
. The result is given in Eq. (
282
). The result for the pole terms, from Eq. (
284
), is

\begin{split}\left[\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}\right]_{p^{2}\to 0}\hskip-42.67912pt&\\
={}&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon^{2}}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{g}}\\
&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}\Bigg[\frac{v-1}{v}-\log\!\left(\frac{v-1}{v+1}\right)\\
&\quad+\log\!\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{4(p\cdot n)^{2}}\right)\Bigg]+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{0})\;.\end{split}

(185)

Here
\gamma_{\mathrm{g}}
is the standard coefficient given in Eq. (
160
). We will combine this result with results from gluon exchange graphs and from quark self-energy graphs in Sec.

.

VIII
The quark self-energy

The one-loop quark self-energy
-{\mathrm{i}}\Sigma(p)
is given by the Feynman diagram shown in Fig.
10
. It can be calculated using using similar techniques to those used for the gluon self-energy, although the calculation is simpler than for the gluon case. One can first find the UV poles of the unrenormalized one-loop self-energy,
\Sigma_{\mathrm{U}}(p)
, with the result (Eq. (
285
))

\begin{split}\Sigma_{\mathrm{U}}(p)={}&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\,C_{\mathrm{F}}\left[\frac{(v-1)^{2}}{v(v+1)}+\frac{\xi}{v}\right]+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{0})\;.\end{split}

(186)

This is the pole that is removed by renormalization and gives the renormalization factor
Z_{\mathrm{q}}
given in Eq. (
162
).

For S-matrix elements involving an initial or final state quark or antiquark, we need the LSZ factor
\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{q}}}
. For this, we need
\Sigma(p)
in the limit
p^{2}\to 0
. Using Eq. (
140
) and the accompanying definition of the Dirac spinor factors, we have

\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{q}}(p)}-1=\left[\frac{\bar{u}(p,s)\Sigma(p)u(p,s)}{2p^{2}}\right]_{p^{2}\to 0}\!\!+\,\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.

(187)

We calculate this with
\xi=1
with a calculation that is similar to the calculation in Appendix
C
for gluons, but somewhat simpler. As for gluons, the result contains infrared double and single poles. The result for the pole terms is

\begin{split}\left[\frac{\bar{u}(p,s)\Sigma(p)u(p,s)}{2p^{2}}\right]_{p^{2}\to 0}\hskip-85.35826pt&\\
={}&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon^{2}}\,C_{\mathrm{F}}-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{q}}\\
&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,C_{\mathrm{F}}\Bigg[\frac{v-1}{v}-\log\!\left(\frac{v-1}{v+1}\right)\\
&\quad+\log\!\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{4(p\cdot n)^{2}}\right)\Bigg]+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{0})\;.\end{split}

(188)

Here
\gamma_{\mathrm{q}}
is the standard coefficient

\gamma_{\mathrm{q}}=\frac{3C_{\mathrm{F}}}{2}\;.

(189)

We will combine this result with results from gluon exchange graphs and from gluon self-energy graphs in Sec.
IX
.

IX
Poles of the S matrix

We have seen that the S matrix for initial or final state external partons has infrared poles in
\epsilon
when we include one virtual loop. Each external parton has a label
l
and can be a T gluon or a massless quark or antiquark. One source of poles is the exchange of a gluon between two of the external partons. From Eq. (
82
), this contribution is

\begin{split}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l}&\sum_{k\neq l}V_{lk}\,\bm{T}_{l}\cdot\bm{T}_{k}\\
={}&-\sum_{l}\sum_{k\neq l}\bm{T}_{l}\cdot\bm{T}_{k}\,\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\log\!\left(\!\frac{-2p_{l}\cdot p_{k}+{\mathrm{i}}0}{\mu^{2}}\!\right)\\
&+\sum_{l}\bm{T}_{l}^{2}\,\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\Bigg\{\frac{v-1}{v}-\log\!\left(\frac{v-1}{v+1}\right)\\
&\quad+\log\!\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{4\,(p_{l}\cdot n)^{2}}\!\right)\Bigg\}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)\;.\end{split}

(190)

The other source of poles is the self-energy graphs, each of which contributes
\sqrt{R_{l}}-1
at order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
. These contributions are given in Eq. (
185
) for gluons and Eq. (
188
) for quarks. They each include a constant
\gamma_{l}
, with
\gamma_{l}=\gamma_{\mathrm{g}}
, Eq. (
160
), if
l
is a gluon and
\gamma_{l}=\gamma_{\mathrm{q}}
, Eq. (
189
), if
l
is a quark. Otherwise, they have the same form, with
\bm{T}_{l}^{2}=C_{\mathrm{A}}
if
l
is a gluon and
\bm{T}_{l}^{2}=C_{\mathrm{F}}
if
l
is a quark. The result is

\begin{split}\sum_{l}(\sqrt{R_{l}}&-1)\\
={}&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\sum_{l}\left[\bm{T}_{l}^{2}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon^{2}}+\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\gamma_{l}\right]\\
&-\sum_{l}\bm{T}_{l}^{2}\,\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\Bigg\{\frac{v-1}{v}-\log\!\left(\frac{v-1}{v+1}\right)\\
&\quad+\log\!\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{4\,(p_{l}\cdot n)^{2}}\!\right)\Bigg\}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)\;.\\
\\
\\
\end{split}

(191)

In the sum of these contributions, the terms involving
v
and
p_{l}\cdot n
cancel, leaving

\begin{split}\sum_{l}&(\sqrt{R_{l}}-1)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l}\sum_{k\neq l}V_{lk}\,\bm{T}_{l}\cdot\bm{T}_{k}\\
={}&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\sum_{l}\left[\bm{T}_{l}^{2}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon^{2}}+\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\gamma_{l}\right]\\
&-\sum_{l}\sum_{k\neq l}\bm{T}_{l}\cdot\bm{T}_{k}\,\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\log\!\left(\!\frac{-2p_{l}\cdot p_{k}+{\mathrm{i}}0}{\mu^{2}}\!\right)\\
&+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{0})+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.\end{split}

(192)

This is the standard result that one finds in Feynman gauge.

X
Conclusions

We have investigated the features of interpolating gauge in QCD or other gauge field theories. This gauge was proposed by Doust
Doust
and Baulieu and Zwanziger
BaulieuZwanziger
as a way to interpolate between a covariant gauge and Coulomb gauge, with the aim of making Coulomb gauge better defined. The attraction of this gauge for us is that it may be useful for QCD constructions in which the infrared singularities of the theory are of paramount interest.

In any gauge, QCD with massless quarks has infrared singularities that appear when a gluon with momentum
q
attaches to an on-shell parton with momentum
p
. First, there is a soft singularity when
q\to 0
. Second, there is a collinear singularity when
q\to\lambda p
with a fixed value of
\lambda
. There are also soft
\times
collinear singularities when
q\to\lambda p
with
\lambda\to 0
. These singularities are important for the subtractions needed in the calculation of cross sections for infrared safe observables in high energy processes. The same singularities are important for the analysis of large logarithms that appear when a process has a hard momentum scale and a much smaller soft momentum scale. The infrared singularities control the large logarithms that appear when one takes the soft scale toward zero. One way of summing these large logarithms is through the use of a parton shower algorithm. It is the extension of parton shower algorithms to use higher order parton splitting functions that provides our principle motivation for investigating interpolating gauge.

As presented in Sec.
II
, interpolating gauge depends on a vector
n
that defines a preferred reference frame and on two parameters,
v
and
\xi
, with
1\leq v<\infty
. With
v=1
, we have a standard covariant gauge, Feynman gauge for
\xi=1
and Lorenz gauge for
\xi=0
. We obtain Coulomb gauge for
v\to\infty
with any
\xi
. We always choose
v>1
except when we want to connect to Feynman gauge. We mostly use
\xi=1
in this paper.

QCD calculations typically use Feynman gauge because of its simplicity. However, in Feynman gauge, there is a problem with collinear singularities. A collinear singularity and a soft
\times
collinear singularity can appear in graphs in which the gluon couples to a far off-shell internal line in a graph. After integrating over the gluon momentum in
4-2\epsilon
dimensions, one obtains poles
1/\epsilon^{2}
and
1/\epsilon
. These poles are unphysical in the sense that they result from the gluon polarization being proportional to its momentum
q
, while a physical gluon has polarization
\varepsilon
that is orthogonal to
q
. Graphs in which a gluon is exchanged between two external partons also have a double pole in Feynman gauge. Again, the double pole is unphysical in that it results from the gluon polarization being proportional to its momentum. One must use Ward identities to sort out these effects, as outlined in Appendix
A
. After using Ward identities, the collinear singularities are effectively associated with self-energy insertions on the external lines.

One could eliminate the collinear singularity problem by choosing a physical gauge, for instance Coulomb gauge. However, as emphasized in Ref.
BaulieuZwanziger
, one then faces a problem with an ambiguity in defining the gauge. To remove this ambiguity in Coulomb gauge, Ref.
BaulieuZwanziger
takes the
v\to\infty
limit of interpolating gauge.

For the uses that we have in mind, there is no need to take a limit
v\to\infty
. As long as
v>1
, the problem with collinear singularities is removed. Any finite value of
v
that is not too close to 1 will do. For instance, one can choose
v=2
.

The attraction of interpolating gauge with
v>1
compared to Feynman gauge is that
for each graph
the collinear singularity problem does not occur. One does not need to apply Ward identities and sum over graphs to bring the collinear singularities into the form of self-energy insertions on the external lines. They have this form from the beginning. We verified this explicitly at one loop order in Secs.
VII
and
VIII
.

The properties of the
v>1
theory that are important for us can be easily understood, as we found in Sec.
III
. The four component gluon field
A^{\mu}(x)
describes two sorts of gluons, each with two components: T gluons and L gluons. The T gluons are transversely polarized and propagate with the speed of light,
c=1
. The L gluons carry the remaining two polarizations and, in the tree-level propagator, propagate with speed
v
in a frame with
n=(1,0,0,0)
. In such a frame, an on-shell L gluon with momentum
q
has
|q^{0}|=v|\vec{q}\,|
. This makes it impossible for an on-shell L gluon to be collinear with an on-shell lightlike particle, with
|p^{0}|=|\vec{p}\,|
. This property eliminates the collinear singularities for L gluons.

We have provided analysis and calculations for some of the important features of interpolating gauge:

•

Ref.
BaulieuZwanziger
argues that the renormalization program works at all orders of perturbation theory in this gauge. In Sec.
VI
, we define the needed renormalization factors
Z
and calculate their order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
contributions from the ultraviolet divergences of one loop graphs.

•

BRST invariance leads to identities for Green functions in interpolating gauge. Ref.
BaulieuZwanziger
used BRST invariance to analyze the renormalization program. In Sec.
V
, we derive identities for the change in Green functions induced by changing the vector
n
and the parameters
v
and
\xi
. We then use these identities to show that the S matrix for quarks and T gluons is invariant under changes of
n
,
v
, and
\xi
.

•

The gluon propagator in interpolating gauge is not Lorentz covariant and has several terms. Consequently, calculations of loop diagrams are not as simple as in Feynman gauge. Nevertheless, we found in Appendix
B
that results can be obtained using Feynman parameterization and numerical integration. Results for the one loop gluon self-energy were shown in Fig.
13
.

•

Poles
1/\epsilon
and
1/\epsilon^{2}
arising from infrared singularities are of particular interest in this paper. Results for gluon exchange between external on-shell partons were presented in Sec.
IV
. Results for the self-energy of an on-shell T gluon were presented in Appendix
C
and Sec.
VII
. Results for the self-energy of an on-shell quark were presented in Sec.
VIII
.

We conclude that there may be practical uses for interpolating gauge.

Appendix A
Infrared singularities in Feynman gauge

In interpolating gauge, all the collinear singularities are located in the self-energy graphs on the external legs. In Feynman gauge, these collinear singularities appear in many graphs and one has to utilize the Ward identity to be able to
factorize them out. This prevents us from being able to define infrared singular functions that match the soft and collinear singularities with one singular function for each graph. In this section we demonstrate these complications at one-loop level.

In interpolating gauge it was natural to decompose the gluon propagator as sum of T and L gluons. In Feynman gauge, we use a different decomposition. We try to separate the pure soft modes, labelled S, from the collinear and soft-collinear modes, labelled C. We write

\begin{split}D^{\mu\nu}(q)={}&-\frac{g^{\mu\nu}}{q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0}=\frac{P_{\mathrm{S}}^{\mu\nu}(q)}{q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0}+\frac{P_{\mathrm{C}}^{\mu\nu}(q)}{q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0}\,.\end{split}

(193)

Here the
P_{\mathrm{S}}^{\mu\nu}(q)
and
P_{\mathrm{C}}^{\mu\nu}(q)
tensors are defined as

\begin{split}P_{\mathrm{S}}^{\mu\nu}(q)={}&P_{T}^{\mu\nu}(q)+\frac{q^{\mu}q^{\nu}+q^{2}n^{\mu}n^{\nu}}{(q\!\cdot\!n)^{2}-q^{2}}\\
={}&-g^{\mu\nu}+\frac{q\!\cdot\!n\,(q^{\mu}n^{\nu}+n^{\mu}q^{\nu})}{(q\!\cdot\!n)^{2}-q^{2}}\;,\\
P_{\mathrm{C}}^{\mu\nu}(q)={}&P_{L}^{\mu\nu}(q)-\frac{q^{\mu}q^{\nu}+q^{2}n^{\mu}n^{\nu}}{(q\!\cdot\!n)^{2}-q^{2}}\\
={}&-\frac{q\!\cdot\!n\,(q^{\mu}n^{\nu}+n^{\mu}q^{\nu})}{(q\!\cdot\!n)^{2}-q^{2}}\,.\end{split}

(194)

Here
(q\cdot n)^{2}-q^{2}=\vec{q}^{\,2}
if we work in a frame in which
n=(1,0,0,0)
. When an internal gluon line becomes on-shell,
q^{2}\to 0
, both parts of the propagator become singular. However, as we shall see,
P_{\mathrm{S}}^{\mu\nu}(q)
and
P_{\mathrm{C}}^{\mu\nu}(q)
contribute differently to soft and to collinear singularities.

At 1-loop level the possible singular graphs with
m
external partons can be written in the form illustrated in Fig.
14
,

\begin{split}\big|M^{(1)}(\{p,&{}f\}_{m})\big\rangle\\
={}&{\mathrm{i}}g\mu^{\epsilon}\sum_{l}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{\bm{T}^{a}_{l}J_{l}^{\mu}(q)\,D_{\mu\nu}(q)}{(p_{l}-q)^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0}\\
&\quad\times\sum_{G}\big\langle{\nu,a}\big|{R_{l}(G;\{p,f\}_{m})}\big\rangle\\
&+\cdots\;.\end{split}

(195)

The ellipsis “
\cdots
” here stands for contributions that do not have leading infrared singularities. In the singular part, external parton
l
, which can be either a quark or a gluon, absorbs a gluon with momentum
q
and color index
a
. Its propagator is
D_{\mu\nu}(q)
. We sum over
l
and integrate over
q
. The gluon couples to a color matrix
\bm{T}^{a}_{l}
and an effective current
J_{l}^{\mu}(q)
, described below. The propagator for parton
l
before the emission has a factor
1/[(p_{l}-q)^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]
, which is singular when
q
is collinear to
p_{l}
or soft. The current
J_{l}^{\mu}(q)
includes either a polarization vector or a Dirac spinor appropriate for the limit
(p_{l}-q)^{2}\to 0
. The complementary polarization vector or spinor is included in the rest of the graph. These on-shell polarization vectors or spinors are indicated by the orthogonal lines on parton line
l
.

The amplitude
\big\langle{\nu,a}\big|{R_{l}(G;\{p,f\}_{m})}\big\rangle
represents the rest of the Feynman graph that contributes to the given process. This is an
m+1
point graph in Feynman gauge. The extra leg is a gluon line with color
a
and polarization index
\nu
. This extra gluon carries the momentum
q^{\mu}
. The external leg
l
of
|R_{l}(G;\{p,f\}_{m})\rangle
caries a momentum of
p_{l}-q
, which is treated as being an on-shell external parton with its appropriate polarization vector or spinor. The dependence on the polarizations or spins of parton
l
is suppressed in the notation.

In
\big\langle{\nu,a}\big|{R_{l}(G;\{p,f\}_{m})}\big\rangle
, the gluon with momentum
q
is connected to any internal line in the graph or to any external leg of the graph except for the leg of parton
l
.

The currents
J_{l}(q)
are matrices
J_{l}(q)_{\hat{s},s}
in the spin space for parton
l
. They also depend on the timelike reference momentum
n
and the momentum and flavor of the parton,
p_{l},f_{l}
, but for the sake of simplicity we hide those arguments and the spin indices. We define

J_{l}^{\mu}(q)_{\hat{s},s}=2p_{l}^{\mu}\delta_{\hat{s},s}-A^{\mu\nu}_{f_{l}}(p_{l})_{\hat{s},s}\,q_{\nu}\;.

(196)

Here the first term appears in the eikonal approximation for soft gluon absorption, while the second term is flavor dependent and has non-trivial dependence on the spins.

For a final state quark, we define
NSI

A^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{q}}(p)_{\hat{s},s}=\frac{\bar{u}(p,s)\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{\nu}{\raise-0.34723pt\hbox to6.00235pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$n$}}\,u(p,\hat{s})}{2p\!\cdot\!n}\;.

(197)

Analogous formulas apply for antiquarks and for initial state quarks and antiquarks.

When parton
l
is a gluon, an extra step is needed
NSsubtractions
. We have a gluon with momentum that we can call
p_{\mathrm{a}}
and Lorentz index
\alpha
and a gluon with momentum that we can call
p_{\mathrm{b}}
and Lorentz index
\beta
combining at a three-gluon vertex to make an on-shell gluon with momentum
p=p_{\mathrm{a}}+p_{\mathrm{b}}
and polarization vector
\varepsilon(p,s)
. There are three terms in the three-gluon vertex, Eq. (
59
). One term is proportional to
g_{\alpha\beta}(p_{\mathrm{b}}-p_{\mathrm{a}})\cdot\varepsilon(p,s)
. Since
p\cdot\varepsilon(p,s)=0
, this term is nonsingular when
p_{\mathrm{a}}
and
p_{\mathrm{b}}
are collinear or either of them is soft. We neglect this term. One term is proportional to
(p+p_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\,\varepsilon_{\alpha}(p,s)
. In this term, we identify
q
in Fig.
14
with
p_{\mathrm{b}}
. The remaining term is proportional to
-(p+p_{\mathrm{a}})_{\alpha}\,\varepsilon_{\beta}(p,s)
. In this term, we identify
q
in Fig.
14
with
p_{\mathrm{a}}
. With this identification, we have

\begin{split}A^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{g}}(p)_{\hat{s},s}={}&g^{\mu\nu}\delta_{s\hat{s}}\;.\end{split}

(198)
