Figure 17:

Illustration of the second term on the right-hand-side of Eq. (
202
). This is the negative of the one term that was not included in Fig.
16
.

The expression in Eq. (
195
) is not immediately usable if we want to define subtraction scheme, since it does not have a factorized form. To obtained such a form we should separate the contributions that apply in the soft and collinear limits. Using the decomposition of the gluon propagator in Eq. (
193
) we
have

\begin{split}\big|M^{(1)}&{}(\{p,f\}_{m})\big\rangle\\
={}&{\mathrm{i}}g\mu^{\epsilon}\sum_{l}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{\bm{T}^{a}_{l}J_{l}^{\mu}(q)\,[P_{\mathrm{S}}(q)]_{\mu\nu}}{[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][(p_{l}-q)^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]}\\
&\quad\times\sum_{G}\big\langle{\nu,a}\big|{R_{l}(G;\{p,f\}_{m}}\big\rangle\\
&+{\mathrm{i}}g\mu^{\epsilon}\sum_{l}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{\bm{T}^{a}_{l}J_{l}^{\mu}(q)\,[P_{\mathrm{C}}(q)]_{\mu\nu}}{[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][(p_{l}-q)^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]}\\
&\quad\times\sum_{G}\big\langle{\nu,a}\big|{R_{l}(G;\{p,f\}_{m})}\big\rangle\\
&+\cdots\;.\end{split}

(199)

We note that the first term cannot be singular in the collinear limit, in which
q
becomes parallel to
p_{l}
, because in this limit
J_{l}(q)^{\mu}\propto q^{\mu}
and
q^{\mu}[P_{\mathrm{C}}(q)]_{\mu\nu}=0
. However, this term can be singular in the soft limit if the other end of the gluon is connected to another external leg, say a leg with index
k
. Since we have only soft singularity, the current can be simplified: it is enough to keep the
2p_{l}^{\mu}
part in Eq. (
196
) since the term
A^{\mu\nu}q_{\nu}
is suppressed by the factor
q
. This leads to the eikonal approximation in the first term of Eq. (
199
), depicted in Fig.
15
.

The second term in Eq. (
199
) can be singular in both the soft and collinear limits. In the limit in which
q
is collinear with
p_{l}
,
J_{l}(q)^{\mu}
is proportional to
q^{\mu}
. Then the term in
[P_{\mathrm{C}}(q)]_{\mu\nu}
proportional to
n_{\mu}q_{\nu}
gives a leading collinear singularity, but the term proportional to
q_{\mu}n_{\nu}
does not contribute because it is suppressed by a factor
q^{2}
. In the limit in which
q
is soft,
q\to 0
, there are two cases to consider. When the soft gluon connects the external parton
l
to an internal line of the graph, there are not enough powers of
1/q
to give a leading singularity.
6
6

6

For an attachment to an internal line, there is a collinear singularity but no soft singularity. However, in one way of organizing the calculation, there is a sum of two soft singularities that cancel. Thus we sometimes speak of having both soft and collinear singularities.
When the soft gluon connects two external partons, there is a leading soft singularity. In this case, there is one graph, but two ends of the gluon line, one with a factor
n_{\mu}
and the other with a factor
q_{\nu}
. We can use this symmetry to let index of the external line connected to
n_{\mu}
be denoted by
l
and the index of the other external line be denoted by something else.

The arguments presented above give for the singular terms in Eq. (
199
),

\begin{split}\big|M^{(1)}&{}(\{p,f\}_{m})\big\rangle\\
={}&4{\mathrm{i}}\pi\,\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\sum_{l<k}\bm{T}_{l}\!\cdot\!\bm{T}_{k}\big|{M^{(0)}(\{p,f\}_{m})}\big\rangle\\
&\times\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{4p_{l}\!\cdot\!P_{\mathrm{S}}(q)\!\cdot\!p_{k}}{[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][(p_{l}-q)^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][(p_{k}+q)^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]}\\
&-{\mathrm{i}}g\mu^{\epsilon}\sum_{l}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{\bm{T}^{a}_{l}\,n_{\mu}J_{l}^{\mu}(q)}{[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][(p_{l}-q)^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]}\\
&\quad\times\sum_{G}\frac{q\!\cdot\!n\,q^{\nu}}{(q\!\cdot\!n)^{2}-q^{2}}\big\langle{\nu,a}\big|{R_{l}(G;\{p,f\}_{m})}\big\rangle\\
&+\cdots\;.\end{split}

(200)

Here the first term, illustrated in Fig.
15
, has a factorized form with one contribution for each graph. In this term,
\big|{M^{(0)}(\{p,f\}_{m})}\big\rangle
is the amplitude without the soft gluon exchange. The integration over the loop momentum can be performed analytically. The second term, illustrated in Fig.
16
, contains a sum over almost every
m+1
parton graph, where the extra parton is a gluon carrying the momentum
q
. The factor
n_{\mu}
is indicated by a diamond shape where the gluon line joins line
l
. The factor
q^{\nu}
is indicated by the open arrow at the end of the gluon line. This extra gluon can connect to every internal or external line in the graph except to parton
l
. Parton
l
carries a momentum of
p_{l}-q
. It becomes on shell either in the soft or the collinear limit. In the singular regions we can apply the Ward identity, as

\begin{split}\sum_{G}q^{\nu}{}&\big\langle{\nu,a}\big|{R_{l}(G;\{p,f\}_{m},\{q,\mathrm{g}\})}\big\rangle\\
={}&g\mu^{\epsilon}\bm{T}_{l}^{a}\big|{M^{(0)}(\{p,f\}_{m})}\big\rangle+\mathcal{O}(q^{2})\;.\end{split}

(201)

This is the negative of the contribution that one would have obtained from an attachment to parton
l
. After using the Ward identity, we can write the singular part of the one-loop amplitudes in factorized form as

\begin{split}\big|M^{(1)}&{}(\{p,f\}_{m})\big\rangle\\
={}&4{\mathrm{i}}\pi\,\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\sum_{l<k}\bm{T}_{l}\!\cdot\!\bm{T}_{k}\big|{M^{(0)}(\{p,f\}_{m})}\big\rangle\\
&\times\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{4p_{l}\!\cdot\!P_{S}(q)\!\cdot\!p_{k}}{[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][(p_{l}-q)^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][(p_{k}+q)^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]}\\
&+4{\mathrm{i}}\pi\,\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\sum_{l}\bm{T}_{l}^{2}\big|{M^{(0)}(\{p,f\}_{m})}\big\rangle\\
&\quad\times\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{n\!\cdot\!J_{l}(q)\,q\!\cdot\!n}{[(q\!\cdot\!n)^{2}-q^{2}]\,[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][(p_{l}-q)^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]}\\
&+\cdots\;.\end{split}

(202)

The first term in Eq. (
202
) is illustrated in Fig.
15
. The second term is illustrated in Fig.
17
.

We note that by taking the limits in Eq. (
201
) and using the Ward identity we might have introduced some spurious UV poles. We have to keep in mind that these UV singularities are fake and they need to be removed.

Now we can perform the integrals, leading to

\begin{split}\big|M^{(1)}(\{p&{},f\}_{m})\big\rangle\\
={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\sum_{l\neq k}\bm{T}_{l}\!\cdot\!\bm{T}_{k}\big|{M^{(0)}(\{p,f\}_{m})}\big\rangle\\
&\quad\times\left\{\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left[\frac{\mu^{2}}{-2p_{l}\!\cdot\!p_{k}}\right]^{\epsilon}-\frac{1}{2\epsilon}\left[\frac{\mu^{2}}{(2p_{l}\!\cdot\!n)^{2}}\right]^{\epsilon}\right.\\
&\quad\qquad\left.-\frac{1}{2\epsilon}\left[\frac{\mu^{2}}{(2p_{k}\!\cdot\!n)^{2}}\right]^{\epsilon}\right\}\\
&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\sum_{l}\bm{T}_{l}^{2}\big|{M^{(0)}(\{p,f\}_{m})}\big\rangle\\
&\quad\times\left\{\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left[\frac{\mu^{2}}{(2p_{l}\!\cdot\!n)^{2}}\right]^{\epsilon}+\frac{2}{1+\delta_{l}}\right\}\\
&+\cdots\;,\end{split}

(203)

where
\delta_{l}=1
if
l
is a gluon otherwise
\delta_{l}=0
. Using color conservation, we can simplify the result even further and obtain the result

\displaystyle\big|{}

\displaystyle M^{(1)}(\{p,f\}_{m})\big\rangle=\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}

\displaystyle\quad\times\bigg\{\sum_{l\neq k}\bm{T}_{l}\!\cdot\!\bm{T}_{k}\frac{1}{\epsilon}\left[\frac{\mu^{2}}{-2p_{l}\!\cdot\!p_{k}}\right]^{\epsilon}-\sum_{l}\frac{2}{1+\delta_{l}}\,\bm{T}_{l}^{2}\bigg\}

\displaystyle\quad\times\big|{M^{(0)}(\{p,f\}_{m})}\big\rangle+\cdots\;.

(204)

This derivation shows that it is quite practical to use Feynman gauge to extract the infrared singularities of amplitudes when we add one gluon exchange to graphs that are either tree graphs or have only hard momenta in loops. However, one faces complications if one wants to extend this method to include more loops with potentially soft or collinear momenta of the partons in the loops. In this case, there are more gluons with propagators
P_{\mathrm{C}}^{\mu\nu}(q)/[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]
. These gluons can couple to each other, so that there are now multiple special cases to be considered when applying the needed Ward identities
BabisCalcs
;
AnastasiouSterman
.

Appendix B
Calculation of the gluon self-energy

We have seen that interpolating gauge offers the advantage that collinear singularities are eliminated in virtual exchange graphs. However, manifest covariance is lost and there are several terms in the gluon propagator. Thus calculations of loop diagrams are not as simple as in Feynman gauge. We have in mind using numerical integration to perform calculations, so perhaps this lack of simplicity in not a crucial problem. In this appendix, we investigate this issue by performing a numerical calculation in interpolating gauge.

We discuss the calculation of the gluon self-energy function
\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)
with a space-like value of
p
, using interpolating gauge with
\xi=1
. The function
\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)
has an ultraviolet pole, which we eliminate by renormalization. It has no infrared poles. Infrared poles will emerge if we take
p^{2}\to 0
.

The unrenormalized (“U”) version of the self-energy function that we wish to calculate has the form

\begin{split}-{\mathrm{i}}\,\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)={}&4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{N^{\mu\nu}(q,p)}{[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][k^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][q\cdot\tilde{q}+{\mathrm{i}}0][k\cdot\tilde{k}+{\mathrm{i}}0]}\;.\end{split}

(205)

Here
d=4-2\epsilon
and the loop momentum is
q
, with
k=p-q
. The numerator function is

\begin{split}N^{\mu\nu}(q,p)={}&-\frac{C_{\mathrm{A}}}{2}\,\Gamma_{\mu\alpha\beta}(-p,q,k)\Gamma_{\nu\gamma\delta}(p,-q,-k)N^{\alpha\gamma}(q)\,N^{\beta\delta}(k)+\frac{C_{\mathrm{A}}}{2}\,q^{2}k^{2}\left[\tilde{q}^{\mu}\tilde{k}^{\nu}+\tilde{k}^{\mu}\tilde{q}^{\nu}\right]\\
&-\frac{C_{\mathrm{A}}}{2}\left[N^{\mu\nu}(k)-g^{\mu\nu}N^{\alpha}_{\alpha}(k)\right]q^{2}q\cdot\tilde{q}-\frac{C_{\mathrm{A}}}{2}\left[N^{\mu\nu}(q)-g^{\mu\nu}N^{\alpha}_{\alpha}(q)\right]k^{2}\,k\cdot\tilde{k}\\
&+4T_{\mathrm{R}}n_{\mathrm{f}}\left[k^{\mu}q^{\nu}+q^{\mu}k^{\nu}-g^{\mu\nu}q\cdot k\right]q\cdot\tilde{q}\,k\cdot\tilde{k}\;.\end{split}

(206)

The second term is for the ghost loop. The third and fourth terms are from the tadpole diagram, symmetrized under
q\leftrightarrow k
. The last term is the quark loop. These contributions are depicted in Fig.
9
. We have defined
\Gamma_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{a},p_{b},p_{c})
using

\Gamma_{\alpha\beta\gamma}^{abc}(p_{a},p_{b},p_{c})=gf_{abc}\Gamma_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{a},p_{b},p_{c})\;.

(207)

Then, from Eq. (
59
),

\Gamma_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{a},p_{b},p_{c})=-\big\{g_{\alpha\beta}(p_{a}-p_{b})_{\gamma}+g_{\beta\gamma}(p_{b}-p_{c})_{\alpha}+g_{\gamma\alpha}(p_{c}-p_{a})_{\beta}\big\}\;.

(208)

We have also defined
N^{\mu\nu}(q)
as

N^{\mu\nu}(q)=q^{2}\,q\cdot\tilde{q}\,D^{\mu\nu}(q)

(209)

with
\xi=1
. From Eq. (
62
), this is

N^{\mu\nu}(q)=-g^{\mu\nu}q\cdot\tilde{q}+q^{\mu}\,\tilde{q}^{\nu}+\tilde{q}^{\mu}\,q^{\nu}-\frac{v^{2}+1}{v^{2}}\,q^{\mu}\,q^{\nu}\;.

(210)

The numerator factor omits a factor
4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\delta_{aa^{\prime}}
, where
a
and
a^{\prime}
are the gluon color indices. The
\delta_{aa^{\prime}}
has been removed from
\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)
and
4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
has been factored out of the numerator function.

It is possible to simplify some parts of the integrand. First, any factors of
q^{2}
,
q\cdot\tilde{q}
,
k^{2}
, or
k\cdot\tilde{k}
in the numerator can be used to cancel the corresponding factors in the denominator, giving a simpler denominator. Second, if the resulting denominator depends only on
q
but not on
k
or depends only on
k
but not on
q
, then we have a scaleless integral. With dimensional regularization, a scaleless integral consists of an ultraviolet pole that exactly cancels an infrared pole. Such scaleless integrals can simply be dropped. However, it is feasible to proceed without implementing any of these simplifications. Then one applies the same general method to all contributions to the integrand. This is the method that we explain below.

We can combine the four denominator factors using three Feynman parameters
x
,
y
and
z
:

\begin{split}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)={}&{\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,N^{\mu\nu}(q,p)\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\ J(x)\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\int_{0}^{1}\!dz\\
&\times\frac{1}{[x(1-y)q^{2}+xyk^{2}+(1-x)(1-z)\,q\cdot\tilde{q}+(1-x)z\,k\cdot\tilde{k}+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{4}}\;,\end{split}

(211)

where

J(x)=4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\,6\,x(1-x)\;.

(212)

To proceed, we manipulate the denominator in Eq. (
211
). We use the projection tensors
P_{+}
and
P_{-}
, Eq. (
20
), and indicate contractions of Lorentz indices with a dot, as in
A\cdot B=C
for
A^{\mu}_{\ \alpha}B^{\alpha}_{\ \nu}=C^{\mu}_{\ \nu}
. The denominator is

\begin{split}D={}&x(1-y)q^{2}+xy(p-q)^{2}+(1-x)(1-z)\,q\cdot\tilde{q}\\
&+(1-x)z\,(p-q)\cdot(\tilde{p}-\tilde{q})\\
={}&q\cdot A(x)\cdot q-2q\cdot A(x)\cdot w(x,y,z)\\
&+xyp^{2}+(1-x)zp\cdot\tilde{p}\;,\end{split}

(213)

where

\begin{split}A(x)={}&\frac{1-x+v^{2}x}{v^{2}}\,P_{+}+P_{-}\;,\\
A(x)^{-1}={}&\frac{v^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\,P_{+}+P_{-}\;,\\
w(x,y,z)={}&A^{-1}(x)\left[xyp+(1-x)z\tilde{p}\right]\;.\end{split}

(214)

Notice that we have combined the terms proportional to
q^{2}
and
q\cdot\tilde{q}
into one term
q\cdot A(x)\cdot q
. Completing the square in the denominator gives

\begin{split}D={}&(q-w(x,y,z))\cdot A(x)\cdot(q-w(x,y,z))\\
&-\Lambda^{2}(x,y,z)\;,\end{split}

(215)

where

\begin{split}\Lambda^{2}(x,y,z)={}&w(x,y,z)\cdot A(x)\cdot w(x,y,z)\\
&-xyp^{2}-(1-x)zp\cdot\tilde{p}\;.\end{split}

(216)

This may be better expressed as

\begin{split}\Lambda^{2}(x,y,z)={}&-\lambda_{0}(x,y,z)\ p^{2}-\lambda_{1}(x,y,z)\ p\cdot\tilde{p}\;,\end{split}

(217)

where

\begin{split}\lambda_{0}(x,y,z)={}&\frac{x(1-x)^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\,(y-z)^{2}+xy(1-y)\;,\\
\lambda_{1}(x,y,z)={}&\frac{x^{2}(1-x)v^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\,(y-z)^{2}\\
&+(1-x)z(1-z)\;.\end{split}

(218)

Notice that
\lambda_{0}(x,y,z)
and
\lambda_{1}(x,y,z)
are positive for
0<x<1
,
0<y<1
,
0<z<1
.

In the integral (
211
), we can shift the integration variable from
q
to
q^{\prime}=q-w
, so that

\begin{split}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)={}&\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\ J(x)\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\int_{0}^{1}\!dz\ {\mathrm{i}}\,\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}q^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{d}}\\
&\times\frac{N^{\mu\nu}(q^{\prime}+w(x,y,z),p)}{[q^{\prime}\cdot A(x)\cdot q^{\prime}-\Lambda^{2}(x,y,z)+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{4}}\;.\end{split}

(219)

Then we can change variables again to
\ell=A^{1/2}(x)q^{\prime}
, with a new jacobian,

J^{\prime}(x)=[(1-x+v^{2}x)/v^{2}]^{-1/2}\;,

(220)

so that

\begin{split}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)={}&\!\!\int_{0}^{1}\!dxJ(x)J^{\prime}(x)\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\int_{0}^{1}\!dz\,{\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\!\int\!\frac{d^{d}\ell}{(2\pi)^{d}}\\
&\times\frac{N^{\mu\nu}(A^{-1/2}(x)\ell+w(x,y,z),p)}{[\ell^{2}-\Lambda^{2}(x,y,z)+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{4}}\;.\end{split}

(221)

We write
N^{\mu\nu}(A^{-1/2}\ell+w,p)
as a function of
\ell
and
p
. We can eliminate terms that are odd in
\ell
because they will integrate to zero. There are then terms in the numerator proportional to 6, 4, 2, and 0 powers of
\ell
. That is, there are terms proportional to
\ell^{\alpha}\ell^{\beta}\ell^{\gamma}\ell^{\delta}\ell^{\rho}\ell^{\sigma}
,
\ell^{\alpha}\ell^{\beta}\ell^{\gamma}\ell^{\delta}
,
\ell^{\alpha}\ell^{\beta}
and 1. We define Lorentz invariant symmetric tensors by

\begin{split}T_{2}^{\alpha\beta}={}&g^{\alpha\beta}\;,\\
T_{4}^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}={}&g^{\alpha\beta}T_{2}^{\gamma\delta}+g^{\alpha\gamma}T_{2}^{\beta\delta}+g^{\alpha\delta}T_{2}^{\beta\gamma}\;,\\
T_{6}^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta\rho\sigma}={}&g^{\alpha\beta}T_{4}^{\gamma\delta\rho\sigma}+g^{\alpha\gamma}T_{4}^{\beta\delta\rho\sigma}+g^{\alpha\delta}T_{4}^{\beta\gamma\rho\sigma}\\
&+g^{\alpha\rho}T_{4}^{\beta\gamma\delta\sigma}+g^{\alpha\sigma}T_{4}^{\beta\gamma\delta\rho}\;.\end{split}

(222)

After integration, we obtain terms proportional to
T_{6}^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta\rho\sigma}
,
T_{4}^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}
,
T_{2}^{\alpha\beta}
and 1. We can use these to define coefficients
A_{0}
,
A_{2}
,
A_{4}
, and
A_{6}
:

\begin{split}A_{0}(\Lambda^{2})={}&{\mathrm{i}}\,\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\!\frac{d^{d}\ell}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{1}{[\ell^{2}-\Lambda^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{4}}\;,\\
A_{2}(\Lambda^{2})T_{2}^{\alpha\beta}={}&{\mathrm{i}}\,\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\!\frac{d^{d}\ell}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{\ell^{\alpha}\ell^{\beta}}{[\ell^{2}-\Lambda^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{4}}\;,\\
A_{4}(\Lambda^{2})T_{4}^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta}={}&{\mathrm{i}}\,\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\!\frac{d^{d}\ell}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{\ell^{\alpha}\ell^{\beta}\ell^{\gamma}\ell^{\delta}}{[\ell^{2}-\Lambda^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{4}}\;,\\
A_{6}(\Lambda^{2})T_{6}^{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta\rho\sigma}={}&{\mathrm{i}}\,\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\!\frac{d^{d}\ell}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{\ell^{\alpha}\ell^{\beta}\ell^{\gamma}\ell^{\delta}\ell^{\rho}\ell^{\sigma}}{[\ell^{2}-\Lambda^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{4}}\;.\end{split}

(223)

The coefficients
A_{J}
are

\begin{split}A_{0}(\Lambda^{2})={}&-\frac{(\epsilon+1)}{6}\,\frac{1}{(\Lambda^{2})^{2}}\,I_{\mathrm{s}}(\Lambda^{2})\;,\\
A_{2}(\Lambda^{2})={}&\frac{1}{12}\,\frac{1}{\Lambda^{2}}\,I_{\mathrm{s}}(\Lambda^{2})\;,\\
A_{4}(\Lambda^{2})={}&-\frac{1}{24}\,\frac{1}{\epsilon}\,I_{\mathrm{s}}(\Lambda^{2})\;,\\
A_{6}(\Lambda^{2})={}&\frac{1}{48}\,\frac{1}{\epsilon(\epsilon-1)}\,\Lambda^{2}\,I_{\mathrm{s}}(\Lambda^{2})\;,\end{split}

(224)

where the standard factor
I_{\mathrm{s}}(\Lambda^{2})
is

\begin{split}I_{\mathrm{s}}(\Lambda^{2})={}&\frac{\Gamma(1+\epsilon)}{(4\pi)^{2-\epsilon}}\,\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{\Lambda^{2}}\right)^{\epsilon}\;.\end{split}

(225)

After integration over
\ell
, we have a result of the form

\begin{split}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)={}&\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\ J(x)\,J^{\prime}(x)\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\int_{0}^{1}\!dz\\
&\times I^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U}}(p;x,y,z)\;.\end{split}

(226)

The
(\ell)^{6}
and
(\ell)^{4}
contributions to
I^{\mu\nu}(p;x,y,z)
are proportional to
1/\epsilon
. The
1/\epsilon
pole is to be removed by renormalization. The
(\ell)^{2}
and
(\ell)^{0}
contributions are finite when
\epsilon\to 0
.

The ultraviolet pole terms are defined by

I^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{pole}}(p;x,y,z)=\left[\epsilon\,I^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U}}(p;x,y,z)\right]_{\epsilon\to 0}\;.

(227)

We remove the poles according to the
\overline{\mathrm{MS}}
prescription by subtracting

I^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{CT}}(p;x,y,z)=\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,I^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{pole}}(p;x,y,z)\;,

(228)

where
S_{\epsilon}
is the standard factor defined in Eq. (
161
).
The renormalized version of
I^{\mu\nu}
is then

\begin{split}I^{\mu\nu}(p;x,&y,z)\\
={}&\big[I^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U}}(p;x,y,z)-I^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{CT}}(p;x,y,z)\big]_{\epsilon\to 0}\;.\end{split}

(229)

The integrand
I^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U}}
has the form

\begin{split}I^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U}}(p;x,y,z;\epsilon)={}&\frac{1}{\epsilon}I_{\mathrm{s}}(\Lambda^{2})\widetilde{I}^{\mu\nu}(p;x,y,z;\epsilon)\\
={}&\frac{1}{(4\pi)^{2}}\frac{(4\pi)^{\epsilon}\Gamma(1+\epsilon)}{\epsilon}\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{\Lambda^{2}}\right)^{\epsilon}\\
&\times\widetilde{I}^{\mu\nu}(p;x,y,z;\epsilon)\;.\end{split}

(230)

This gives us

\begin{split}I^{\mu\nu}(p;x,y,z)={}&\frac{1}{(4\pi)^{2}}\widetilde{I}^{\mu\nu}(p;x,y,z;0)\log\!\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{\Lambda^{2}}\right)\\
&+\frac{1}{(4\pi)^{2}}\left[\frac{d\widetilde{I}^{\mu\nu}(p;x,y,z;\epsilon)}{d\epsilon}\right]_{\epsilon=0}\;.\end{split}

(231)

For the parts of
I^{\mu\nu}
that did not have a pole
1/\epsilon
, this prescription gives simply the contribution to
I^{\mu\nu}
evaluated at
\epsilon=0
.

The renormalized version of
\Pi^{\mu\nu}
is then obtained by integrating
I^{\mu\nu}
over the Feynman parameters:

\begin{split}\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)={}&\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\ J(x)\,J^{\prime}(x)\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\int_{0}^{1}\!dz\\
&\times I^{\mu\nu}(p;x,y,z)\;,\end{split}

(232)

This integral can be performed by numerical integration. Typical results are reported in Fig.
13
.

The pole term in
\Pi^{\mu\nu}
is

\begin{split}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{pole}}(p)={}&\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\ J(x)\,J^{\prime}(x)\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\int_{0}^{1}\!dz\\
&\times I^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{pole}}(p;x,y,z)\;.\end{split}

(233)

The integrals over the Feynman parameters can be performed analytically, giving

\begin{split}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{pole}}(p)={}&C_{1}(v)\left\{g^{\mu\nu}p^{2}-p^{\mu}p^{\nu}\right\}\\
&+C_{2}(v)\left\{2h^{\mu\nu}p^{2}-\tilde{p}^{\mu}p^{\nu}-p^{\mu}\tilde{p}^{\nu}\right\}\;,\end{split}

(234)

where

\begin{split}C_{1}(v)={}&\frac{C_{\mathrm{A}}\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{-11v^{3}-16v^{2}-7v+2}{3v(v+1)^{2}}\\
&+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{4}{3}\,T_{\mathrm{R}}n_{\mathrm{f}}\;,\\
C_{2}(v)={}&\frac{C_{\mathrm{A}}\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{2v(2v+1)}{3(v+1)^{2}}\;.\end{split}

(235)

This calculation has been for
\xi=1
. This result for the ultraviolet pole matches the more general result in Eq. (
177
) at
\xi=1
.

Appendix C
The gluon self-energy with
p^{2}\to 0

We now investigate the one-loop self-energy for a T gluon that is an external particle in the S matrix. This means that we need not the full
\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)
but only
\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)\varepsilon_{\nu}(p,s)
. Given the tensor structure (
182
) of
\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)
, we see that
\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)\varepsilon_{\nu}(p,s)
is proportional to
\varepsilon^{\mu}(p,s)
. Thus it suffices to consider
\varepsilon_{\mu}(p,s)\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)\varepsilon_{\nu}(p,s)
. Since an external T gluon is on its mass shell, and is accompanied by a tree level propagator proportional to
1/p^{2}
, the quantity that we need for the S matrix, Eq. (
V.6
), is the first order contribution to
\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{g}}}
, the square root of the residue of the T-gluon propagator at
p^{2}=0
. This is

\Pi_{\mathrm{IR}}=\lim_{p^{2}\to 0}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}(p,s)\Pi^{\mu\nu}(p)\varepsilon_{\nu}(p,s)}{2p^{2}}\;.

(236)

The factor
1/2
gives us the order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
contribution to
\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{g}}}
instead of
R_{\mathrm{g}}
. In taking the limit
p^{2}\to 0
, we start with
p^{2}<0
.

Some care is required in calculating
\Pi_{\mathrm{IR}}
because taking the limit
p^{2}\to 0
leads to infrared divergences. We maintain the dimensional regulation of the calculation with
d=4-2\epsilon
, with
\epsilon<0
so that we regulate an infrared divergence. We take the limit
p^{2}\to 0
in Eq. (
236
). Then we let
\epsilon\to 0
, giving poles
1/\epsilon^{2}
and
1/\epsilon
plus a finite
\epsilon^{0}
contribution. The finite contribution then contains logarithms of the dimensional regularization scale
\mu^{2}
. Knowing the IR pole terms and the scale dependence is just what one wants for use in a parton shower algorithm.

Fortunately,
\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}\varepsilon_{\nu}
is much simpler than the full
\Pi^{\mu\nu}
. This simplicity enables us to manipulate the integrand for
\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}\varepsilon_{\nu}
so that all of the IR poles can be extracted, leaving only one integral for the coefficient of a finite part that remains for numerical integration.

The unrenormalized self-energy function that we wish to calculate is given by the form that we used in Eq. (
205
),

\begin{split}\varepsilon_{\mu}(p,s)\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)\varepsilon_{\nu}(p,s)={}&4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\,{\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}(p,s)N^{\mu\nu}(q,p)\varepsilon_{\nu}(p,s)}{[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][k^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][q\cdot\tilde{q}+{\mathrm{i}}0][k\cdot\tilde{k}+{\mathrm{i}}0]}\;.\end{split}

(237)

After some manipulation, we can write the numerator in the form

\begin{split}\varepsilon_{\mu}N^{\mu\nu}\varepsilon_{\nu}={}&N_{1}+N_{2}+N_{3}+N_{4}+N_{5}+\mathrm{scaleless}\,,\end{split}

(238)

where “scaleless” denotes contributions that give scaleless integrals, which vanish in dimensional regularization, and where

\begin{split}N_{1}={}&\left\{c_{1,1}(q\cdot\varepsilon)^{2}+c_{1,2}\,p^{2}\right\}q\cdot\tilde{q}\ k\cdot\tilde{k}\;,\\
N_{2}={}&c_{2}\,p^{2}\,(q\cdot\varepsilon)^{2}\,k\cdot\tilde{k}\;,\\
N_{3}={}&c_{3}\,p^{2}\,q\cdot\tilde{p}\ k\cdot\tilde{k}\;,\\
N_{4}={}&\left\{c_{4,1}\,p^{2}\,p\cdot\tilde{p}+c_{4,2}\,(p^{2})^{2}\,\right\}\,(q\cdot\varepsilon)^{2}\;,\\
N_{5}={}&c_{5}\,(p^{2})^{2}\,k\cdot\tilde{k}\;.\end{split}

(239)

Here we have defined coefficients

\begin{split}c_{1,1}={}&4C_{\mathrm{A}}(1-\epsilon)-8T_{\mathrm{R}}n_{\mathrm{f}}\;,\\
c_{1,2}={}&-4C_{\mathrm{A}}+2T_{\mathrm{R}}n_{\mathrm{f}}\;,\\
c_{2}={}&-2C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{v^{2}-1}{v^{2}}\;,\\
c_{3}={}&4C_{\mathrm{A}}\;,\\
c_{4,1}={}&C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{v^{2}-1}{v^{2}}\;,\\
c_{4,2}={}&-C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{v^{4}-1}{2v^{4}}\;,\\
c_{5}={}&-C_{\mathrm{A}}\frac{v^{2}+1}{v^{2}}\;.\end{split}

(240)

We analyze each of these contributions in turn.

We begin with the contribution from
N_{1}
:

\begin{split}\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},1}\varepsilon_{\nu}\!={}&4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\,{\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\!\int\!\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{c_{1,1}(q\cdot\varepsilon)^{2}\!+c_{1,2}\,p^{2}}{[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][k^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]}.\end{split}

(241)

We can write this as an integral over a Feynman parameter
x
as

\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},1}\varepsilon_{\nu}={}

\displaystyle 4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\,{\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\int_{0}^{1}\!dx

\displaystyle\times\frac{c_{1,1}(q\cdot\varepsilon)^{2}+c_{1,2}\,p^{2}}{[(1-x)q^{2}+xk^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{2}}\;.

(242)

Using
k=p-q
, this is

\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},1}\varepsilon_{\nu}={}

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\,4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\,{\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,

\displaystyle\times\frac{c_{1,1}(q\cdot\varepsilon)^{2}+c_{1,2}\,p^{2}}{[(q-xp)^{2}+x(1-x)p^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{2}}\;.

(243)

We change variables to
\ell=q-xp
and use
\varepsilon\cdot p=0
to obtain

\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},1}\varepsilon_{\nu}={}

\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\,4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\,{\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}\ell}{(2\pi)^{d}}

\displaystyle\times\frac{c_{1,1}(\ell\cdot\varepsilon)^{2}+c_{1,2}\,p^{2}}{[\ell^{2}+x(1-x)p^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{2}}\;.

(244)

We can perform the integration over
\ell
using

\displaystyle{\mathrm{i}}\,\mu^{2\epsilon}\!\int\frac{d^{d}\ell}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{1}{[\ell^{2}-\Lambda^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{2}}={}

\displaystyle-\frac{1}{\epsilon}\,I_{\mathrm{s}}(\Lambda^{2})\;,

\displaystyle{\mathrm{i}}\,\mu^{2\epsilon}\!\int\frac{d^{d}\ell}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{\ell^{\mu}\ell^{\nu}}{[\ell^{2}-\Lambda^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{2}}={}

\displaystyle-\frac{\Lambda^{2}I_{\mathrm{s}}(\Lambda^{2})}{2\epsilon(1-\epsilon)}\,g^{\mu\nu},

(245)

where
I_{\mathrm{s}}(\Lambda^{2})
was defined in Eq. (
225
). This gives

\displaystyle\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},1}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}

\displaystyle-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\!\int_{0}^{1}\!\!dx\,\frac{x(1-x)c_{1,1}+(1-\epsilon)c_{1,2}}{2\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}

\displaystyle\times\Gamma(1+\epsilon)\left(\frac{-x(1-x)p^{2}}{4\pi\,\mu^{2}}\right)^{-\epsilon}\;.

(246)

We take
-p^{2}>0
and take the limit
p^{2}\to 0
at a fixed value of
\epsilon
with
\epsilon<0
. This gives us

\begin{split}\lim_{p^{2}\to 0}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},1}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&0\;.\end{split}

(247)

Next, we turn to the contribution proportional to
N_{2}
:

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},2}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&\frac{c_{2}}{2}\,4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\,{\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{(q\cdot\varepsilon)^{2}}{[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][k^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][q\cdot\tilde{q}+{\mathrm{i}}0]}\;.\end{split}

(248)

We can write this as an integral over a Feynman parameters
x
and
y
as

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},2}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&\frac{c_{2}}{2}\,4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\,{\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\,2x\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\,\frac{(q\cdot\varepsilon)^{2}}{[x(1-y)q^{2}+xyk^{2}+(1-x)q\cdot\tilde{q}+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{3}}\;.\end{split}

(249)

With
k=p-q
, this is

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},2}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&c_{2}\,4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\ x\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\ {\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{(\varepsilon\cdot q)^{2}}{[(q-w(x,y,0))\cdot A(x)\cdot(q-w(x,y,0))-\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{3}}\;.\end{split}

(250)

Here
A(x)
and
w(x,y,z)
were defined in Eq. (
214
) and
\Lambda^{2}(x,y,z)
was defined in Eq. (
217
). We change variables to
q^{\prime}=q-w
, noting that
\varepsilon\cdot w=0
since
\varepsilon\cdot p=0
. Then we change variables to
\ell=A^{1/2}(x)q^{\prime}
, with a Jacobian
J^{\prime}(x)
given in Eq. (
220
). Since
\varepsilon\cdot n=0
we have
\varepsilon\cdot q^{\prime}=\varepsilon\cdot\ell
. This gives

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},2}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&c_{2}\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\ x\left[\frac{v^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\right]^{1/2}\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\ 4\pi{\mathrm{i}}\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\,\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}\ell}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{(\varepsilon\cdot\ell)^{2}}{[\ell^{2}-\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{3}}\;.\end{split}

(251)

We can perform the
\ell
integration using

\begin{split}{\mathrm{i}}\,\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}\ell}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{\ell^{\mu}\ell^{\nu}}{[\ell^{2}-\Lambda^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{3}}={}&-g^{\mu\nu}\ \frac{1}{4}\,\frac{1}{\epsilon}\,I_{\mathrm{s}}(\Lambda^{2})\;.\end{split}

(252)

This gives us

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},2}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&c_{2}\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\ x\left[\frac{v^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\right]^{1/2}\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\ \frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{\Gamma(1+\epsilon)}{4\epsilon}\left(\frac{4\pi\mu^{2}}{\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)}\right)^{\epsilon}\;.\end{split}

(253)

It is straightforward to take the limit
p^{2}\to 0
. At
p^{2}=0
we have from Eq. (
217
),

\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)=-\frac{x^{2}(1-x)y^{2}v^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\,p\cdot\tilde{p}\;.

(254)

Thus

\begin{split}\lim_{p^{2}\to 0}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},2}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{\Gamma(1+\epsilon)}{4\epsilon}\,\left(\frac{4\pi\mu^{2}}{-p\cdot\tilde{p}}\right)^{\epsilon}c_{2}\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\ x\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\ \left[\frac{v^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\right]^{1/2}\left(\frac{1-x+v^{2}x}{x^{2}(1-x)y^{2}v^{2}}\right)^{\epsilon}\;.\end{split}

(255)

This has a
1/\epsilon
pole and a finite part as
\epsilon\to 0
. After performing the integrals over
y
and
x
, we find

\begin{split}\lim_{p^{2}\to 0}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},2}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{c_{2}}{4}\,\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{-p\cdot\tilde{p}}\right)^{\epsilon}\left\{\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,I_{2,1}(v)+2I_{2,1}(v)+I_{2,2}(v)\right\}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{0})\;.\end{split}

(256)

The factor
(\mu^{2}/(-p\cdot\tilde{p}))^{\epsilon}
can be expanded to give a contribution proportional to
\log(\mu^{2}/(-p\cdot\tilde{p}))
. The needed integrals are

\begin{split}I_{2,1}(v)={}&\frac{2v(v+2)}{3(v+1)^{2}}\;,\\
I_{2,2}(v)={}&\!\frac{4v}{9(v^{2}-1)^{2}}\bigg((5-3\log(2))v^{3}-3v^{2}-\!(12-9\log(2))v+10\\
&\quad+3v(v^{2}-3)\log\!\left[\frac{v+1}{v}\right]+6\log\!\left[\frac{(v+1)^{2}}{4v}\right]\!\bigg).\end{split}

(257)

For
v=2
,
I_{2,1}(2)=0.592593
and
I_{2,2}(2)=1.28204
.

We are now ready to consider the contribution proportional to
N_{3}
:

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},3}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\,\frac{c_{3}}{2}\,{\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{q\cdot\tilde{p}}{[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][k^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][q\cdot\tilde{q}+{\mathrm{i}}0]}\;.\end{split}

(258)

We can write this as an integral over a Feynman parameters
x
and
y
and rearrange the denominator as for
\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},2}\varepsilon_{\nu}
, giving

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},3}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&c_{3}\,\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\ x\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\ 4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\,{\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{q\cdot\tilde{p}}{[(q-w(x,y,0))\cdot A(x)\cdot(q-w(x,y,0))-\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{3}}\;.\end{split}

(259)

We change variables to
q^{\prime}=q-w
. Then in the numerator,
q\cdot\tilde{p}=q^{\prime}\cdot\tilde{p}+w\cdot\tilde{p}
, but we can drop
q^{\prime}\cdot\tilde{p}
since it is odd under
q^{\prime}\to-q^{\prime}
. Then we change variables to
\ell=A^{1/2}(x)q^{\prime}
, with a Jacobian
J^{\prime}(x)
. This gives

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},3}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&c_{3}\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\ x\left[\frac{v^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\right]^{1/2}\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\ 4\pi{\mathrm{i}}\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\,\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}\ell}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{w(x,y,0)\cdot\tilde{p}}{[\ell^{2}-\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{3}}\;.\end{split}

(260)

We can perform the
\ell
integration using

\begin{split}{\mathrm{i}}\,\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}\ell}{(2\pi)^{d}}\frac{1}{[\ell^{2}-\Lambda^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0]^{3}}={}&\frac{I_{\mathrm{s}}(\Lambda^{2})}{2\Lambda^{2}}\,\;.\end{split}

(261)

This gives us

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},3}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&\frac{c_{3}}{2}\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\Gamma(1+\epsilon)\!\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\,x\left[\frac{v^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\right]^{1/2}\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\,\frac{w(x,y,0)\cdot\tilde{p}}{\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)}\left(\frac{4\pi\mu^{2}}{\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)}\right)^{\epsilon}.\end{split}

(262)

It is straightforward to take the limit
p^{2}\to 0
. At
p^{2}=0
,
\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)
is given by Eq. (
254
). For
w(x,y,0)\cdot\tilde{p}
at
p^{2}=0
, we use Eqs. (
214
), (
24
), (
22
), and (
20
) to derive

w(x,y,0)\cdot\tilde{p}=-\frac{\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)}{(1-x)y}\;.

(263)

This gives us

\begin{split}\lim_{p^{2}\to 0}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},3}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&-\frac{c_{3}}{2}\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\Gamma(1+\epsilon)\left(\frac{4\pi\mu^{2}}{-p\cdot\tilde{p}}\right)^{\epsilon}\int_{0}^{1}\!\frac{dy}{y^{1+2\epsilon}}\int_{0}^{1}\!\frac{dx}{(1-x)^{1+\epsilon}}\,\left[\frac{v^{2}x^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\right]^{1/2-\epsilon}.\end{split}

(264)

The
y
-integration is trivial and gives a factor
-1/(2\epsilon)
. The
x
-integration produces another
1/\epsilon
from the endpoint
x\to 1
. This gives a double pole, a single pole, and a finite contribution as
\epsilon\to 0
. The integrals over
x
and
y
needed for these contributions can be performed analytically, giving

\begin{split}\lim_{p^{2}\to 0}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},3}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&-\frac{c_{3}}{4}\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}[1+\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}\epsilon^{2}]\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{-p\cdot\tilde{p}}\right)^{\epsilon}\left\{\frac{1}{\epsilon}+I_{3,1}+\epsilon\left(I_{3,2}-\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}\right)\right\}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)\;.\end{split}

(265)

The integrals
I_{3,1}
and
I_{3,2}
are given below. We have included the standard factor
S_{\epsilon}
and compensated by multiplying by

\Gamma(1+\epsilon)\Gamma(1-\epsilon)=1+\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}\epsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{4})\;.

(266)

This gives

\begin{split}\lim_{p^{2}\to 0}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},3}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&-\frac{c_{3}}{4}\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{-p\cdot\tilde{p}}\right)^{\epsilon}\left\{\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon^{2}}+\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}I_{3,1}(v)+I_{3,2}(v)\right\}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)\;.\end{split}

(267)

The factor
(\mu^{2}/(-p\cdot\tilde{p}))^{\epsilon}
can be expanded to give contributions proportional to powers of
\log(\mu^{2}/(-p\cdot\tilde{p}))
. The needed integrals are

\begin{split}I_{3,1}(v)={}&\frac{2v}{v+1}-2\log\left(\frac{2v}{v+1}\right)\\
I_{3,2}(v)={}&\frac{8v}{v+1}+\frac{4v}{v^{2}-1}\,\log\left(\frac{2}{v+1}\right)-\frac{4v}{v+1}\,\log\left(\frac{2v}{v+1}\right)+\log(2)\log\left(\frac{2v^{2}(v-1)^{2}}{(v+1)^{4}}\right)+2\left[\log\left(\frac{v}{v+1}\right)\right]^{2}\\
&+\left[\log\left(v\right)\right]^{2}+\log(v+1)\log\left(\frac{v+1}{(v-1)^{2}}\right)-2\,\mathrm{Li}_{2}\left(-\frac{2}{v-1}\right)+2\,\mathrm{Li}_{2}\left(-\frac{v+1}{v-1}\right)+2\,\mathrm{Li}_{2}\left(-\frac{1}{v}\right)\\
&-2\,\mathrm{Li}_{2}\left(\frac{v-1}{2v}\right)+2\,\mathrm{Li}_{2}\left(\frac{v-1}{v}\right)+2\,\mathrm{Li}_{2}\left(-\frac{v-1}{v+1}\right)-2\,\mathrm{Li}_{2}\left(\frac{v-1}{v+1}\right)\;.\end{split}

(268)

For
v=2
,
I_{3,1}(2)=0.757969
and
I_{3,2}(2)=1.27310

The contribution proportional to
N_{4}
is quite simple. We start with

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},4}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&\frac{4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{2}\,{\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{[c_{4,1}\,p\cdot\tilde{p}+c_{4,2}\,p^{2}](q\cdot\varepsilon)^{2}}{[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][k^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][q\cdot\tilde{q}+{\mathrm{i}}0][k\cdot\tilde{k}+{\mathrm{i}}0]}\;.\end{split}

(269)

We can evaluate this using the method of Appendix
B
. We introduce integrations over Feynman parameters
x
,
y
, and
z
. Then we change integration variables from
q
to
\ell=A^{1/2}(x)(q-w(x,y,z))
. The analysis is simpler than for the general contribution in Appendix
B
because, since
\varepsilon\cdot p=\varepsilon\cdot n=0
, we have
q\cdot\varepsilon=\ell\cdot\varepsilon
. After performing the
\ell
-integration, we have

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},4}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{\Gamma(1+\epsilon)}{4}\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\ x(1-x)\left[\frac{v^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\right]^{1/2}\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\int_{0}^{1}\!dz\ \frac{c_{4,1}\,p\cdot\tilde{p}+c_{4,2}\,p^{2}}{\Lambda^{2}(x,y,z)}\left(\frac{4\pi\mu^{2}}{\Lambda^{2}(x,y,z)}\right)^{\epsilon}\;.\end{split}

(270)

We take the
p^{2}\to 0
limit of this by simply setting
p^{2}=0
in the integral. The integral over the Feynman parameters does not produce any poles in
\epsilon
, so we can simply set
\epsilon=0
. This gives

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},4}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{c_{4,1}}{4}\,I_{4}(v)+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)\;,\end{split}

(271)

where

\begin{split}I_{4}(v)={}&\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\ x(1-x)\left[\frac{v^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\right]^{1/2}\\
&\times\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\int_{0}^{1}\!dz\left[\frac{v^{2}x}{1-x+v^{2}x}\,x(1-x)(y-z)^{2}+(1-x)z(1-z)\right]^{-1}\;.\end{split}

(272)

As far as we can see, this integral cannot be expressed in closed form using logarithms and dilogarithms. For
v=2
, it is
I_{4}(2)=3.67765
.

The contribution proportional to
N_{5}
vanishes. To see why, we begin with

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},5}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&4\pi\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}\,\frac{c_{5}}{2}\,{\mathrm{i}}\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\,\frac{p^{2}}{[q^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][k^{2}+{\mathrm{i}}0][q\cdot\tilde{q}+{\mathrm{i}}0]}\;.\end{split}

(273)

We introduce an integral over Feynman parameters
x
and
y
and then integrate over the loop momentum as for
\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},3}\varepsilon_{\nu}
. This leads to

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},5}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{c_{5}}{2}\,\Gamma(1+\epsilon)\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\left[\frac{v^{2}x^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\right]^{1/2}\int_{0}^{1}\!dy\ \frac{p^{2}}{\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)}\left(\frac{4\pi\mu^{2}}{\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)}\right)^{\epsilon}\;.\end{split}

(274)

We want the limit of this as
p^{2}\to 0
. There is a factor of
p^{2}
in the numerator, but this factor multiplies an integral that diverges if we set
\epsilon
to zero, so we should be cautious about taking the
p^{2}\to 0
limit inside the integral. The function
\Lambda^{2}
is, from Eq. (
217
),

\begin{split}\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)={}&-\left[\frac{x(1-x)^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\,y^{2}+xy(1-y)\right]p^{2}-\frac{v^{2}x^{2}(1-x)}{1-x+v^{2}x}\,y^{2}\,p\cdot\tilde{p}\;.\end{split}

(275)

In the limit
p^{2}\to 0
, the integral over
y
is dominated by very small
y
. To capture this behavior, we integrate over
y
from 0 to
\infty
instead of from 0 to 1 and approximate
\Lambda^{2}
by

\begin{split}\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)\approx{}&-xy\,p^{2}-\frac{v^{2}x^{2}(1-x)}{1-x+v^{2}x}\,y^{2}\,p\cdot\tilde{p}\;.\end{split}

(276)

We change integration variables from
y
to
y^{\prime}
defined by

y^{\prime}\,p^{2}=y\,p\cdot\tilde{p}\;.

(277)

Then

\begin{split}\Lambda^{2}(x,y,0)\approx{}&=\frac{-(p^{2})^{2}}{p\cdot\tilde{p}}\left[xy^{\prime}+\frac{v^{2}x^{2}(1-x)}{1-x+v^{2}x}\,y^{\prime\,2}\right]\;.\end{split}

(278)

This gives us

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},5}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}\approx{}&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{c_{5}}{2}\left[\frac{-(p^{2})^{2}}{4\pi\mu^{2}\,p\cdot\tilde{p}}\right]^{-\epsilon}\!\Gamma(1+\epsilon)\int_{0}^{1}\!dx\left[\frac{v^{2}x^{2}}{1-x+v^{2}x}\right]^{1/2}\!\int_{0}^{\infty}\!dy^{\prime}\left[xy^{\prime}+\frac{v^{2}x^{2}(1-x)}{(1-x)+v^{2}x}\,y^{\prime\,2}\right]^{-1-\epsilon}\!.\end{split}

(279)

We take the limit
p^{2}\to 0
with
\epsilon<0
. The factor
[-p^{2}]^{-2\epsilon}
vanishes while the integrals over
x
and
y
are finite. Thus

\left[\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U},5}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}\right]_{p^{2}\to 0}=0\;.

(280)

The contributions derived above give us the unrenormalized
\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{U}}\varepsilon_{\nu}/(2p^{2})
. We have to subtract the ultraviolet counterterms, which we can obtain from Eq. (
177
):

\begin{split}\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}_{\mathrm{CT}}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\frac{c_{\mathrm{A}}(v,1)+\tilde{c}_{\mathrm{A}}(v,1)}{2}=\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\left\{C_{\mathrm{A}}\frac{3v^{3}+12v^{2}+7v-2}{6v(v+1)^{2}}-\frac{2}{3}\,T_{\mathrm{R}}n_{\mathrm{f}}\right\}\;.\end{split}

(281)

The sum of these contributions is the renormalized
\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}\varepsilon_{\nu}/(2p^{2})
:

\begin{split}\left[\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}\right]_{p^{2}\to 0}={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\Bigg\{\frac{c_{2}}{4}\,\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{-p\cdot\tilde{p}}\right)^{\epsilon}\left\{\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,I_{2,1}(v)+2I_{2,1}(v)+I_{2,2}(v)\right\}\\
&-\frac{c_{3}}{4}\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{-p\cdot\tilde{p}}\right)^{\epsilon}\left\{\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon^{2}}+\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}I_{3,1}(v)+I_{3,2}(v)\right\}+\frac{c_{4,1}}{4}\,I_{4}(v)\\
&-\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\frac{c_{\mathrm{A}}(v,1)+\tilde{c}_{\mathrm{A}}(v,1)}{2}\Bigg\}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)\;.\end{split}

(282)

It is of interest to collect the single and double pole terms. We write
-p\cdot\tilde{p}
at
p^{2}=0
using Eq. (
25
) as
(v^{2}-1)/v^{2}](p\cdot n)^{2}
. This gives

\begin{split}\left[\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}\right]_{p^{2}\to 0}={}&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon^{2}}\,\frac{c_{3}}{4}\\
&+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\Bigg[\frac{c_{2}}{4}\,I_{2,1}(v)-\frac{c_{3}}{4}\,I_{3,1}(v)-\frac{c_{3}}{4}\log\!\left(\frac{v^{2}\mu^{2}}{(v^{2}-1)(p\cdot n)^{2}}\right)-\frac{c_{\mathrm{A}}(v,1)+\tilde{c}_{\mathrm{A}}(v,1)}{2}\Bigg]\\
&+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{0})\;.\end{split}

(283)

Using Eqs. (
165
), (
240
), (
257
), and (
268
) for the values for the coefficients here, we obtain

\begin{split}\left[\frac{\varepsilon_{\mu}\Pi^{\mu\nu}\varepsilon_{\nu}}{2p^{2}}\right]_{p^{2}\to 0}={}&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon^{2}}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\gamma_{\mathrm{g}}\\
&+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\Bigg[-\frac{v-1}{v}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}+C_{\mathrm{A}}\log\!\left(\frac{v-1}{v+1}\right)-C_{\mathrm{A}}\log\!\left(\frac{\mu^{2}}{4(p\cdot n)^{2}}\right)\Bigg]\\
&+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{0})\;.\end{split}

(284)

Here
\gamma_{\mathrm{g}}
is the standard coefficient defined in Eq. (
160
). The double and single pole terms in the first line of Eq. (
284
) match the standard result for the pole terms in the S matrix in Feynman gauge. The terms in the second line will cancel against the gluon contributions to the
\bm{T}_{l}\cdot\bm{T}_{l}
terms from gluon exchange graphs.

Appendix D
Renormalization calculations

In Sec.
VI
, we saw how the UV pole terms in the gluon self-energy diagrams in interpolating gauge lead to the one-loop contributions to the renormalization factors
Z_{A}
,
Z_{v}
and
Z_{\xi}
. In this appendix, we outline the structure of some of the other UV divergent one loop diagrams and see how the UV pole terms lead to the remaining renormalization factors
Z
reported in Sec.
VI
.

We expand each renormalization factor in powers of
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
as
Z=1+\delta Z+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})
and
(Z_{A})^{\mu}_{\nu}=g^{\mu}_{\nu}+(\delta Z_{A})^{\mu}_{\nu}+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})
, where
\delta Z
contains one power of
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
. We compute one loop quantities like the renormalized quark self-energy function
\Sigma(p)
that are proportional to one power of
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
and depend on gauge parameters
v
and
\xi
. The unrenormalized version is denoted by
\Sigma_{\mathrm{U}}(p)
. This is the same as this quantity in the bare theory,
\Sigma_{\mathrm{B}}(p)
, except that we use the renormalized
g
,
v
and
\xi
. Since
g=g_{\mathrm{B}}(1+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}))
,
v=v_{\mathrm{B}}(1+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}))
, and
\xi=\xi_{\mathrm{B}}(1++\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}))
, changing from bare to renormalized
g
,
v
and
\xi
does not affect the result at order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
.

D.1
Quark self-energy

A straightforward calculation of the one loop diagram in Fig.
10
for the unrenormalized quark self-energy
-{\mathrm{i}}\Sigma_{\mathrm{U}}
gives the UV pole

\begin{split}\Sigma_{\mathrm{U}}(p)={}&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\,C_{\mathrm{F}}\left[\frac{(v-1)^{2}}{v(v+1)}+\frac{\xi}{v}\right]+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{0})\;.\end{split}

(285)

The inverse of the quark propagator is
{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}-\Sigma(p)
at order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
, where
\Sigma(p)
is the renormalized quark self-energy. This gives us the relation

\left[{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}-\Sigma_{\mathrm{U}}(p)\right]=Z_{\psi}^{-1}\left[{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}-\Sigma(p)\right]+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.

(286)

Then

{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}-\Sigma_{\mathrm{U}}(p)={\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}-\Sigma(p)-\delta Z_{\psi}\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}\;.

(287)

This gives us

\delta Z_{\psi}\,{\raise-1.31944pt\hbox to5.03125pt{\hss/\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$p$}}=\Sigma_{\mathrm{U}}(p)-\Sigma(p)\;.

(288)

We use our result Eq. (
285
) for the pole term in
\Sigma_{\mathrm{U}}(p)
and note that by definition the renormalized
\Sigma(p)
has no pole. This gives

\delta Z_{\psi}=-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,C_{\mathrm{F}}\left[\frac{(v-1)^{2}}{v(v+1)}+\frac{\xi}{v}\right]\;.

(289)

This is the result reported in Eq. (
162
).

D.2
Ghost self-energy

The determination of
\delta Z_{\eta}
for the ghost field is slightly more subtle. A straightforward calculation of the one loop diagram in Fig.
11
for the unrenormalized ghost self-energy
-{\mathrm{i}}\Pi^{\mathrm{ghost}}_{\mathrm{U}}
gives the UV pole

\begin{split}\Pi^{\mathrm{ghost}}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)\hskip-17.07182pt&\\
={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}\Big\{\left[\frac{16v^{2}+v+1}{12v(v+1)}-\frac{\xi}{4v}\right]\,p\cdot\tilde{p}\\
&\quad-\frac{2(2v+1)(v-1)}{3v^{3}(v+1)}\,(p\cdot n)^{2}\Big\}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{0})\;.\end{split}

(290)

The inverse of the ghost propagator is
p\cdot\tilde{p}-\Pi^{\mathrm{ghost}}(p)
at order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
. This gives us

\begin{split}p\cdot\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{B}}-\Pi^{\mathrm{ghost}}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)={}&Z_{\eta}^{-1}(p\cdot\tilde{p}-\Pi^{\mathrm{ghost}}(p))+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.\end{split}

(291)

Here
\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{B}}=(h_{\mathrm{B}})^{\mu}_{\nu}p^{\nu}
is defined using a factor
1/v_{\mathrm{B}}^{2}
in
(h_{\mathrm{B}})^{\mu}_{\nu}
, with
h^{\mu}_{\nu}
as in Eq. (
22
). Since
1/v_{\mathrm{B}}^{2}=Z_{v}^{-1}/v^{2}
, we have

\begin{split}p\cdot\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{B}}={}&\frac{Z_{v}^{-1}-1}{v^{2}}(p\cdot n)^{2}+p\cdot\tilde{p}\;.\end{split}

(292)

This gives us

\begin{split}p\cdot\tilde{p}+\frac{Z_{v}^{-1}-1}{v^{2}}\,(p\cdot n)^{2}-\Pi^{\mathrm{ghost}}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)\hskip-85.35826pt&\\
={}&Z_{\eta}^{-1}(p\cdot\tilde{p}-\Pi^{\mathrm{ghost}}(p))+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{0})\;.\end{split}

(293)

Expanding the renormalization factors to order
\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}
gives

\begin{split}p\cdot\tilde{p}-\frac{\delta Z_{v}}{v^{2}}\,&(p\cdot n)^{2}-\Pi^{\mathrm{ghost}}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)\\
={}&p\cdot\tilde{p}-\delta Z_{\eta}\,p\cdot\tilde{p}-\Pi^{\mathrm{ghost}}(p)\;.\end{split}

(294)

Thus

\begin{split}\delta Z_{\eta}\,p\cdot\tilde{p}={}&\Pi^{\mathrm{ghost}}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)-\Pi^{\mathrm{ghost}}(p)+\frac{\delta Z_{v}}{v^{2}}\,(p\cdot n)^{2}\;.\end{split}

(295)

We can use Eq. (
290
) for the pole term in
\Pi^{\mathrm{ghost}}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)
. We already know
\delta Z_{v}
from the gluon self-energy. It is given in Eq. (
167
). Using these results, we have

\begin{split}\delta Z_{\eta}\,p\cdot\tilde{p}={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}C_{\mathrm{A}}\bigg\{\left[\frac{16v^{2}+v+1}{12v(v+1)}-\frac{\xi}{4v}\right]p\cdot\tilde{p}\\
&\quad-\frac{2(2v+1)(v-1)}{3v^{3}(v+1)}\,(p\cdot n)^{2}\bigg\}\\
&+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}\frac{2(2v+1)(v-1)}{3v^{3}(v+1)}(p\cdot n)^{2}.\end{split}

(296)

The terms proportional to
(p\cdot n)^{2}
cancel, leaving

\begin{split}\delta Z_{\eta}={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}\left[\frac{16v^{2}+v+1}{12v(v+1)}-\frac{\xi}{4v}\right]\;.\end{split}

(297)

This is the result reported in Eq. (
163
).

D.3
Quark-gluon vertex

We use the graphs in Fig.
12
to calculate the unrenormalized one-loop quark gluon vertex function,
-{\mathrm{i}}g\Gamma^{\mu}_{\mathrm{U}}(p)
,

\begin{split}\Gamma^{\mu}_{\mathrm{U}}={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\gamma_{\mu}\bigg[C_{\mathrm{F}}\left(\frac{(v-1)^{2}}{v(v+1)}+\frac{\xi}{v}\right)\\
&\quad+C_{\mathrm{A}}\frac{3v^{2}+2v+1}{3v(v+1)^{2}}+C_{\mathrm{A}}\frac{\xi-1}{4v}\bigg]\\
&\quad+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\tilde{\gamma}^{\mu}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}\frac{2v(1+2v)}{3(v+1)^{2}}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{0})\;.\end{split}

(298)

The (renormalized) quark-gluon amputated three point function divided by
g
is
\gamma^{\mu}+\Gamma^{\mu}(p)+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})
. To apply renormalization, we use,

\gamma^{\mu}+\Gamma_{\mathrm{U}}^{\mu}=[Z_{A}^{-1/2}]^{\mu}_{\nu}Z^{-1}_{\psi}Z^{-1}_{g}(\gamma^{\nu}+\Gamma^{\nu})+\mathcal{O}(\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.

(299)

Writing
Z=1+\delta Z
in each case, this is

\begin{split}\gamma^{\mu}+\Gamma_{\mathrm{U}}^{\mu}={}&\gamma^{\mu}+\Gamma^{\mu}\\
&-\frac{1}{2}\,[\delta Z_{A}]^{\mu}_{\nu}\gamma^{\nu}-\delta Z_{\psi}\gamma^{\mu}-\delta Z_{g}\gamma^{\mu}\;.\end{split}

(300)

That is

\begin{split}\Gamma_{\mathrm{U}}^{\mu}-\Gamma^{\mu}={}&-\frac{1}{2}\,[\delta Z_{A}]^{\mu}_{\nu}\gamma^{\nu}-\delta Z_{\psi}\gamma^{\mu}-\delta Z_{g}\gamma^{\mu}\;.\end{split}

(301)

Given our result (
298
) for
\Gamma^{\mu}_{\mathrm{U}}
and using our previous results (
164
) for
Z_{A}
and (
162
)
Z_{\psi}
, we have

\begin{split}&\hbox to141.55pt{\vbox to117.27pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 70.88661pt\lower-68.1349pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

Figure 18:

Diagrams for the one loop contributions to the three gluon vertex function.

\begin{split}\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,&\gamma^{\mu}\left[C_{\mathrm{F}}\left(\frac{(v-1)^{2}}{v(v+1)}+\frac{\xi}{v}\right)+C_{\mathrm{A}}\frac{3v^{2}+2v+1}{3v(v+1)^{2}}+C_{\mathrm{A}}\frac{\xi-1}{4v}\right]+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\tilde{\gamma}^{\mu}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}\frac{2v(1+2v)}{3(v+1)^{2}}\\
={}&+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\gamma^{\mu}\left\{-C_{\mathrm{A}}\left[\frac{22v^{3}+35v^{2}+20v-1}{12v(v+1)^{2}}-\frac{\xi}{4v}\right]+\frac{2}{3}\,T_{\mathrm{R}}n_{\mathrm{f}}\right\}+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\tilde{\gamma}^{\mu}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{2v(2v+1)}{3(v+1)^{2}}\\
&+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\gamma^{\mu}\,C_{\mathrm{F}}\left(\frac{(v-1)^{2}}{v(v+1)}+\frac{\xi}{v}\right)-\delta Z_{g}\gamma^{\mu}\;.\end{split}

(302)

The coefficients of
\tilde{\gamma}^{\mu}
and the coefficients of
C_{\mathrm{F}}
match. We can solve for
\delta Z_{g}
:

\delta Z_{g}=\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\left[-\frac{11}{6}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}+\frac{2}{3}\,T_{\mathrm{R}}n_{\mathrm{f}}\right]\;.

(303)

Note that this is independent of
v
and
\xi
. This is the result reported in Eq. (
159
).

D.4
Three gluon vertex

We can check how the renormalization program is working by calculating the three gluon vertex function at one loop order. We call the one-particle-irreducible three-gluon Green function
\Gamma^{abc}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{a},p_{b},p_{c})
, where the momenta are directed out of the vertex function. We define
\Gamma_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{a},p_{b},p_{c})
by

\Gamma^{abc}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{a},p_{b},p_{c})=gf_{abc}\Gamma_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{a},p_{b},p_{c})\;.

(304)

Our aim is to calculate the ultraviolet pole terms in
\Gamma_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{a},p_{b},p_{c})
. In this appendix, we denote the zero loop version,
\Gamma_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{a},p_{b},p_{c})
, Eq. (
207
), by
\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{a},p_{b},p_{c})
.

The graphs needed for
\Gamma^{abc}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{a},p_{b},p_{c})
are illustrated in Fig.
18
. We write the integral for the graph with a single gluon loop as

\begin{split}gf_{abc}&\Gamma_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{\mathrm{a}},p_{\mathrm{b}},p_{\mathrm{c}})\\
={}&g^{3}\,f_{a\bar{c}\bar{b}}f_{b\bar{a}\bar{c}}f_{c\bar{b}\bar{a}}\,\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\!\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}\\
&\times\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}_{\alpha\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}(p_{\mathrm{a}},q_{\mathrm{c}},-q_{\mathrm{b}})\\
&\times\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}_{\beta\beta_{1}\beta_{2}}(p_{\mathrm{b}},q_{\mathrm{a}},-q_{\mathrm{c}})\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}_{\gamma\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}}(p_{\mathrm{c}},q_{\mathrm{b}},-q_{\mathrm{a}})\\
&\times{\mathrm{i}}D^{\alpha_{1}\beta_{2}}(q_{\mathrm{c}})\,{\mathrm{i}}D^{\beta_{1}\gamma_{2}}(q_{\mathrm{a}})\,{\mathrm{i}}D^{\gamma_{1}\alpha_{2}}(q_{\mathrm{b}})\;.\end{split}

(305)

Here the momenta on the three sides of the loop are related to the loop momentum
q
by
NSsubtractions

\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{a}}={}

\displaystyle q+\frac{p_{\mathrm{c}}-p_{\mathrm{b}}}{3}\;,

\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{b}}={}

\displaystyle q+\frac{p_{\mathrm{a}}-p_{\mathrm{c}}}{3}\;,

(306)

\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{c}}={}

\displaystyle q+\frac{p_{\mathrm{b}}-p_{\mathrm{a}}}{3}\;.

We sum over the three graphs that have a four-gluon vertex. The graph in which gluons b and c join at the four-gluon vertex is illustrated in Fig.
18
. This graph is

\displaystyle gf_{abc}

\displaystyle\Gamma_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{\mathrm{a}},p_{\mathrm{b}},p_{\mathrm{c}})

\displaystyle={}

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mu^{2\epsilon}\int\!\frac{d^{d}q}{(2\pi)^{d}}

\displaystyle\times gf_{a\bar{c}\bar{b}}\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}_{\alpha\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}(p_{\mathrm{a}},q_{\mathrm{c}},-q_{\mathrm{b}})\,{\mathrm{i}}D^{\alpha_{1}\bar{\gamma}}(q_{\mathrm{c}}){\mathrm{i}}D^{\bar{\beta}\alpha_{2}}(q_{\mathrm{b}})

\displaystyle\times(-{\mathrm{i}}g^{2})\Big\{f_{\bar{a}bc}f_{\bar{a}\bar{b}\bar{c}}[g_{\beta\bar{\beta}}g_{\gamma\bar{\gamma}}-g_{\beta\bar{\gamma}}g_{\gamma\bar{\beta}}]

\displaystyle\quad\quad+f_{\bar{a}b\bar{c}}f_{\bar{a}c\bar{b}}[g_{\beta\gamma}g_{\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}-g_{\beta\bar{\beta}}g_{\gamma\bar{\gamma}}]

\displaystyle\quad\quad+f_{\bar{a}b\bar{b}}f_{\bar{a}c\bar{c}}[g_{\beta\gamma}g_{\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}-g_{\beta\bar{\gamma}}g_{\gamma\bar{\beta}}]\Big\}\;.

(307)

The momenta on the two sides of the loop are related to the loop momentum
q
by
NSsubtractions

\begin{split}q_{\mathrm{b}}={}&q+\frac{1}{2}\,p_{\mathrm{a}}\;,\\
q_{\mathrm{c}}={}&q-\frac{1}{2}\,p_{\mathrm{a}}\;.\end{split}

(308)

We express the integrals needed for the graphs in Fig.
18
using Feynman parameter representations, along the lines of Appendix
B
. This allows us to extract the ultraviolet pole terms in the form

\begin{split}\Gamma_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{\mathrm{a}},p_{\mathrm{b}},p_{\mathrm{c}})={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\Big\{A\big[g_{\alpha\beta}(p_{\mathrm{a}}-p_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+g_{\beta\gamma}(p_{\mathrm{b}}-p_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+g_{\gamma\alpha}(p_{\mathrm{c}}-p_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\big]\\
&\quad\quad+B\big[h_{\alpha\beta}(p_{\mathrm{a}}-p_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+h_{\beta\gamma}(p_{\mathrm{b}}-p_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+h_{\gamma\alpha}(p_{\mathrm{c}}-p_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\big]\\
&\quad\quad+C\big[g_{\alpha\beta}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{a}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+g_{\beta\gamma}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{b}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+g_{\gamma\alpha}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{c}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\big]\\
&\quad\quad+D\big[h_{\alpha\beta}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{a}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+h_{\beta\gamma}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{b}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+h_{\gamma\alpha}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{c}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\big]\Big\}\;.\end{split}

(309)

For the gluon loop graph, we find

\displaystyle A={}

\displaystyle-C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{5v^{4}+15v^{3}+9v^{2}+23v+12}{6v(v+1)^{3}}-C_{\mathrm{A}}\frac{9(\xi-1)}{8v}\;,

\displaystyle B={}

\displaystyle-C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{v(2v^{2}+3v+7)}{12(v+1)^{3}}\;,

\displaystyle C={}

\displaystyle-C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{v(10v^{2}-3v+5)}{12(v+1)^{3}}\;,

\displaystyle D={}

\displaystyle-C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{v}{24}\;.

(310)

For the ghost loop graph, we find

\displaystyle A={}

\displaystyle 0\;,

\displaystyle B={}

\displaystyle 0\;,

\displaystyle C={}

\displaystyle 0\;,

\displaystyle D={}

\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{v}{24}\;.

(311)

For the graphs with a four-gluon vertex, we find

\displaystyle A={}

\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{(3v+1)(3v^{3}+6v^{2}+3v+2)}{2v(v+1)^{3}}+C_{\mathrm{A}}\frac{3(\xi-1)}{8v}\;,

\displaystyle B={}

\displaystyle-C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{v(10v^{2}+15v+3)}{4(v+1)^{3}}\;,

\displaystyle C={}

\displaystyle-C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{v(2v^{2}+9v+1)}{4(v+1)^{3}}\;,

\displaystyle D={}

\displaystyle 0\;.

(312)

For the graphs with a quark loop, we find

\displaystyle A={}

\displaystyle-\frac{4}{3}\,T_{\mathrm{R}}n_{\mathrm{f}}\;,

\displaystyle B={}

\displaystyle 0\;,

\displaystyle C={}

\displaystyle 0\;,

\displaystyle D={}

\displaystyle 0\;.

(313)

For the sum of all graphs, we find

\displaystyle A={}

\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{A}}\left(\frac{11}{3}-\frac{3v^{2}+2v+1}{v(v+1)^{2}}-\frac{3(\xi-1)}{4v}\right)-\frac{4}{3}\,T_{\mathrm{R}}n_{\mathrm{f}}\;,

\displaystyle B={}

\displaystyle-C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{4v(2v+1)}{3(v+1)^{2}}\;,

\displaystyle C={}

\displaystyle-C_{\mathrm{A}}\,\frac{2v(2v+1)}{3(v+1)^{2}}\;,

\displaystyle D={}

\displaystyle 0\;.

(314)

The renormalization factors
Z
have already been defined. We now check whether these renormalization factors
Z
provide the counterterms needed to remove these poles. Renormalizing the gluon field gives

\begin{split}\Gamma^{abc}_{\mathrm{B},\alpha\beta\gamma}(g_{\mathrm{B}})={}&(Z_{\mathrm{A}}^{-1/2})^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\alpha}(Z_{\mathrm{A}}^{-1/2})^{\bar{\beta}}_{\beta}(Z_{\mathrm{A}}^{-1/2})^{\bar{\gamma}}_{\gamma}\Gamma^{abc}_{\bar{\alpha}\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}(g)\;,\end{split}

(315)

where the subscript B denotes the vertex function in the bare theory and
g_{\mathrm{B}}
is the bare coupling. This gives us

\begin{split}\Gamma^{abc}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(g)={}&(Z_{\mathrm{A}}^{1/2})^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\alpha}(Z_{\mathrm{A}}^{1/2})^{\bar{\beta}}_{\beta}(Z_{\mathrm{A}}^{1/2})^{\bar{\gamma}}_{\gamma}\\
&\times\left[g_{\mathrm{B}}f_{abc}\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}_{\bar{\alpha}\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}+\Gamma^{\mathrm{loop},abc}_{\mathrm{B},\bar{\alpha}\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}(g)\right]\;.\end{split}

(316)

In the first term, we can use
g_{\mathrm{B}}=Z_{g}g
. In the second term, we can replace
g_{\mathrm{B}}
by
g
since we work only to order
g^{3}
. This is then the full one loop three point function but without its renormalization counterterms, which we denote by a subscript U for
unrenormalized
. Thus

\begin{split}\Gamma^{abc}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(g)={}&(Z_{\mathrm{A}}^{1/2})^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\alpha}(Z_{\mathrm{A}}^{1/2})^{\bar{\beta}}_{\beta}(Z_{\mathrm{A}}^{1/2})^{\bar{\gamma}}_{\gamma}Z_{\mathrm{g}}gf_{abc}\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}_{\bar{\alpha}\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}\\
&+\Gamma^{\mathrm{loop},abc}_{\mathrm{U},\bar{\alpha}\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}(g)+\mathcal{O}(g\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.\end{split}

(317)

To order
g^{3}
, this is

\begin{split}\Gamma^{abc}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(g)={}&\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree},abc}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(g)+\left(\frac{1}{2}\,g^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\alpha}g^{\bar{\beta}}_{\beta}(\delta Z_{\mathrm{A}})^{\bar{\gamma}}_{\gamma}+\frac{1}{2}\,g^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\alpha}(\delta Z_{\mathrm{A}})^{\bar{\beta}}_{\beta}g^{\bar{\gamma}}_{\gamma}+\frac{1}{2}\,(\delta Z_{\mathrm{A}})^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\alpha}g^{\bar{\beta}}_{\beta}g^{\bar{\gamma}}_{\gamma}+g^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\alpha}g^{\bar{\beta}}_{\beta}g^{\bar{\gamma}}_{\gamma}\delta Z_{g}\right)gf_{abc}\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}_{\bar{\alpha}\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}\\
&+\Gamma^{\mathrm{loop},abc}_{\mathrm{U},\bar{\alpha}\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}(g)+\mathcal{O}(g\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.\end{split}

(318)

For the renormalization factors, we use Eqs. (
164
) and (
159
)

\begin{split}(\delta Z_{\mathrm{A}})^{\mu}_{\nu}={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\left[c_{\mathrm{A}}(v,\xi)g^{\mu}_{\nu}+\tilde{c}_{\mathrm{A}}(v,\xi)h^{\mu}_{\nu}\right]\;,\\
\delta Z_{g}={}&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\gamma_{\mathrm{g}}\;.\end{split}

(319)

This gives us

\begin{split}\Gamma^{abc}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(g)-\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree},abc}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(g)={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\left[\frac{3}{2}\,c_{\mathrm{A}}(v,\xi)-\gamma_{\mathrm{g}}\right]gf_{abc}\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}\\
&+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\frac{1}{2}\,\tilde{c}_{\mathrm{A}}(v,\xi)\left(g^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\alpha}g^{\bar{\beta}}_{\beta}h^{\bar{\gamma}}_{\gamma}+g^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\alpha}h^{\bar{\beta}}_{\beta}g^{\bar{\gamma}}_{\gamma}+h^{\bar{\alpha}}_{\alpha}g^{\bar{\beta}}_{\beta}g^{\bar{\gamma}}_{\gamma}\right)\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}_{\bar{\alpha}\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}\,gf_{abc}\\
&+\Gamma^{\mathrm{loop},abc}_{\mathrm{U},\bar{\alpha}\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}(g)+\mathcal{O}(g\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.\end{split}

(320)

We use Eqs. (
165
) and (
160
),

\begin{split}\frac{3}{2}c_{\mathrm{A}}(v,\xi)-\gamma_{\mathrm{g}}={}&\left(\frac{11}{3}-\frac{3v^{2}+2v+1}{v(v+1)^{2}}-\frac{3(\xi-1)}{4v}\right)C_{\mathrm{A}}-\frac{4}{3}\,T_{\mathrm{R}}n_{\mathrm{f}}\;,\\
\tilde{c}_{\mathrm{A}}(v,\xi)={}&-\frac{4v(2v+1)}{3(v+1)^{2}}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}\;,\end{split}

(321)

and the structure of
\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree}}
from Eq. (
207
). This gives

\begin{split}\Gamma^{abc}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(g)-\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree},abc}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(g)={}&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\left[\left(\frac{11}{3}-\frac{3v^{2}+2v+1}{v(v+1)^{2}}-\frac{3(\xi-1)}{4v}\right)C_{\mathrm{A}}-\frac{4}{3}\,T_{\mathrm{R}}n_{\mathrm{f}}\right]gf_{abc}\\
&\times\left\{g_{\alpha\beta}(p_{\mathrm{a}}-p_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+g_{\beta\gamma}(p_{\mathrm{b}}-p_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+g_{\gamma\alpha}(p_{\mathrm{c}}-p_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\right\}\\
&+\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\,\frac{2v(2v+1)}{3(v+1)^{2}}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}gf_{abc}\Big\{2h_{\alpha\beta}(p_{\mathrm{a}}-p_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+2h_{\beta\gamma}(p_{\mathrm{b}}-p_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+2h_{\gamma\alpha}(p_{\mathrm{c}}-p_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\\
&\quad\quad+g_{\alpha\beta}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{a}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+g_{\beta\gamma}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{b}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+g_{\gamma\alpha}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{c}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\Big\}\\
&+\Gamma^{\mathrm{loop},abc}_{\mathrm{U},\bar{\alpha}\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}(g)+\mathcal{O}(g\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;.\end{split}

(322)

This is

\Gamma^{abc}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(g)=\Gamma^{\mathrm{tree},abc}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(g)+\Gamma^{\mathrm{loop},abc}_{\mathrm{U},\bar{\alpha}\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}(g)-\Gamma^{\mathrm{loop},abc}_{\mathrm{CT},\bar{\alpha}\bar{\beta}\bar{\gamma}}(g)+\mathcal{O}(g\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}^{2})\;,

(323)

where

\begin{split}\Gamma^{\mathrm{loop},abc}_{\mathrm{CT},\alpha\beta\gamma}(g)={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\left[\left(\frac{11}{3}-\frac{3v^{2}+2v+1}{v(v+1)^{2}}-\frac{3(\xi-1)}{4v}\right)C_{\mathrm{A}}-\frac{4}{3}\,T_{\mathrm{R}}n_{\mathrm{f}}\right]gf_{abc}\\
&\times\left[g_{\alpha\beta}(p_{\mathrm{a}}-p_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+g_{\beta\gamma}(p_{\mathrm{b}}-p_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+g_{\gamma\alpha}(p_{\mathrm{c}}-p_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\right]\\
&-\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\,\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\frac{2v(2v+1)}{3(v+1)^{2}}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}gf_{abc}\Big\{2h_{\alpha\beta}(p_{\mathrm{a}}-p_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+2h_{\beta\gamma}(p_{\mathrm{b}}-p_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+2h_{\gamma\alpha}(p_{\mathrm{c}}-p_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\\
&\quad\quad+g_{\alpha\beta}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{a}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+g_{\beta\gamma}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{b}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+g_{\gamma\alpha}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{c}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\Big\}\;.\end{split}

(324)

We can write this as

\begin{split}\Gamma_{\mathrm{CT},\alpha\beta\gamma}(p_{\mathrm{a}},p_{\mathrm{b}},p_{\mathrm{c}})={}&\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{s}}}{4\pi}\frac{S_{\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\Big\{A\big[g_{\alpha\beta}(p_{\mathrm{a}}-p_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+g_{\beta\gamma}(p_{\mathrm{b}}-p_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+g_{\gamma\alpha}(p_{\mathrm{c}}-p_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\big]\\
&\quad\quad+B\big[h_{\alpha\beta}(p_{\mathrm{a}}-p_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+h_{\beta\gamma}(p_{\mathrm{b}}-p_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+h_{\gamma\alpha}(p_{\mathrm{c}}-p_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\big]\\
&\quad\quad+C\big[g_{\alpha\beta}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{a}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+g_{\beta\gamma}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{b}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+g_{\gamma\alpha}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{c}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\big]\\
&\quad\quad+D\big[h_{\alpha\beta}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{a}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{b}})_{\gamma}+h_{\beta\gamma}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{b}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{c}})_{\alpha}+h_{\gamma\alpha}(\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{c}}-\tilde{p}_{\mathrm{a}})_{\beta}\big]\Big\}\;.\end{split}

(325)

Then

\begin{split}A={}&\left(\frac{11}{3}-\frac{3v^{2}+2v+1}{v(v+1)^{2}}-\frac{3(\xi-1)}{4v}\right)C_{\mathrm{A}}-\frac{4}{3}\,T_{\mathrm{R}}n_{\mathrm{f}}\;,\\
B={}&-\frac{4v(2v+1)}{3(v+1)^{2}}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}\;,\\
C={}&-\frac{2v(2v+1)}{3(v+1)^{2}}\,C_{\mathrm{A}}\;,\\
D={}&0\;.\end{split}

(326)

We see that the counterterms exactly cancel the pole terms in Eq. (
D.4
).
